sas.summary: Spurs are such heavy title favorites that one loss can't drop 'em. But as Brent Barry notes: ''I guess we can put to rest all those rumors about us going undefeated.''
The injuries and two heavy road defeats on consecutive Saturdays are indeed worrying, but here's the pick-me-up: Duncan is shooting 84.2 percent at the line.
Finley is back, Ginobili is healing and Spurs' Saturday hex is over. But there's no change at the top because Pistons get same one-loss grace period Spurs got.
Never thought I'd see these Spurs, after a pretty focused start, losing at home to Chicago or dropping this low. Not without a catastrophic injury.

Manu, in Pop's words, was ''just starting to play great.'' But they're better off bringing him back slowly, because Spurs have the depth to do so now ... and because they have to have a healthy Manu in the springtime.

Remember a week or so ago when Pop said it's too early in such a long season ''to go after these guys'' like he wants to? Just a hunch, but it'll be harder for Pop to hold back after going to lowly Atlanta and losing.
Hard to imagine a better Manu insurance policy than Finley. But a string of tight games with Manu out  suggests Spurs lack an edge no matter how hot his stand-in is.
A loss at Detroit, with Manu missing, isn't the most alarming development, but Spurs' sense of urgency seems to be missing, too. And that shouldn't depend on Manu.
Now that Manu is back, after Spurs went 7-3 without him, we can proceed to the next big issue. Our official position: Duncan shouldn't have shaved his head.
Just a hunch, but I'm guessing Spurs don't mind one bit that their 26 wins (yes, same as Detroit's total) are generating very little attention/scrutiny/hoopla.
The real scares? Detroit's board domination in the two games (113-62) and fears that Duncan's mobility won't get any better until he gets offseason rest.
With four quality wins after the Detroit debacle, Spurs don't drop because of their play. They drop because their second most important player keeps getting hurt.
Duncan and Ginobili aren't playing at full strength, true. But nothing has changed: Every team in the league outside of Detroit would trade for Spurs' problems.
Spurs never sweat a stretch of eight straight roadies in February, but this (cushy?) Rodeo Road Trip comes with five days of rest back home after a 3-0 start.
Spurs have found more than cohesion and momentum on their Rodeo Road Trip. They've also found the old Manu, who sure looked like his All-Star self in Indy.
Dismiss them at your own peril. As fragile as Spurs seem with Duncan and Manu at less than 100 percent, they're on pace to break the franchise record for wins (62).
It hasn't really hurt, with Spurs right on Mavs' heels, but this is the lowest-scoring month (14.6 ppg) in Duncan's career. Previous low: 15.2 ppg in November 1997.
For all its big-game experience, Spurs still will get a confidence boost from beating Dallas -- and denting Mavs' confidence -- after losing two 'big' games to Pistons.
In case you doubted Duncan's discomfort, perhaps you saw Friday's box score: TD had 12 points, Luke Walton had 13 for visiting (and victorious) Lakers.
If yet another win vs. Phoenix didn't say Best in the West to you, how 'bout this: Spurs have only six losses in conference play. Mavs are next with 11.
A 2-2 week doesn't sound so great, but Spurs did start the week by beating Warriors at home. That's something Heat, Mavs and Kings wish they could say this month.
Maybe he is feeling better: Duncan has scored 20 or more points in seven of the past 11 games. Before that? Just four times in all of 2006.
One home loss to Dallas, big as it was, isn't the big concern. The big concern continues to be whether Duncan/Ginobili/Spurs are healthy enough to repeat.
Brent Barry is right when he says all the doom and gloom surrounding Spurs is a bit much, because they can still secure the best record in club history with a 2-0 finish.

det.summary: The opposition hasn't been top-shelf, true, but the transition to the new coach seems to be off to a rather smooth, focused start.

Talk about perfect starts. For fuel, undefeated Pistons have also convinced themselves that they're still getting no respect from the outside world when, in truth, everyone around the league is raving about them.
Every team has two or three games per season like Saturday's in Dallas. You can stomach it a little easier when you show up for that nightmare undefeated.
By the standards of their start, Pistons should have swept the week. That said, they still beat two teams (Nuggets, Bucks) in pretty good form and still belong up here.

Remember last week when we wrote that Pistons rated the first 18 games to be the toughest portion of their schedule? If they're right, then everyone else in the East can only hope that they start getting bored.
Pistons might well reside in the league's toughest division. Yet even in the Central, can you say that any team is close to them right now?
The near-perfect start just got a little closer to perfect: To go with its sparkly record, Detroit gets to watch its two main East rivals deal with drama earlier than expected.
You can look it up: Only one team since 1970 has crafted a better 25-game start than Detroit. You guessed it: Bulls, at 23-2, in their 72-win season.
Can't quite call it a devastating defeat in Cleveland. It means Pistons are only on a 70-12 pace now, six games ahead of their nearest East chaser.
Well ... now we know the team Pistons least want to see in the Finals. A second straight loss to Utah -- yes, Utah -- leaves our trusty No. 1 on a mere 69-13 pace.
Only thing left for Pistons to prove now, after spanking Spurs again, is that their iron-man starting five can stay healthy for the rest of the season.
In case you've stopped paying attention, Pistons could soon match Tigers' famed 35-5 start in 1984. Which figures to reignite the 70-win talk, like it or not.
Trying to keep it fresh with those ''boring'' Pistons, we steal this line from Bernie Bickerstaff: ''Most teams have a go-to player. They have a go-to team.''
When Chicago lost two straight in its 72-win season, it took Bulls from 41-3 to 41-5. Pistons' 2-2 week sets them back a bit farther; Detroit is at only a 70-win pace now.
Yes, even Dr. Detroit (as one loyal reader calls me) can drop the hammer. Pistons plunge two spots after letting me down in Atlanta and another two-loss week.
Health and holding off Mavs and Spurs for home-court advantage are all that matter now. Unless you think Pistons have a 28-3 run in them.
Calm down, Motown. Mavs stay at No. 1 because they're on an 18-1 run. Besides, your Pistons are starving for bulletin-board material these days.
A 22-1 finish gets 'em to 70 wins, but weary Pistons would settle for home-court advantage throughout the playoffs (at any number) and some rest for the starters.
Since a 20-0 finish falls under the heading of ''unlikely,'' Pistons will have to settle for being the season's first team to 50 wins. First to 60? We'll see.
Losing to New York, in Knicks' current state of turmoil, is an undeniable two-spot strike against last week's No. 1. And, yes, we factored in the ejections.
So does the week we just witnessed mean Pistons would rather face Miami than New Jersey in the Eastern Conference finals? Just throwing it out there.
Beating Heat, Mavs and Suns in relatively quick succession takes Pistons to 9-4 against the rest of the top six ... and takes them back to No. 1.
Not going to win 70, obviously, but Pistons were indeed first to 60 wins and have a healthy three-game lead with five to play in the race for best overall record.
Focus on falling short of 70 wins, if you wish, but this is Pistons' best regular season ever ... with home-court advantage and a deeper bench to bring to the playoffs.

ind.summary: Shaq goes down against Indy, Pacers escape Miami with a win ... and then it's Pacers who stumble at home to Philly the next time out? Huh?
Maybe my expectations are too high, especially this early, but I reckon Pacers should be 6-0. Doubt they'd disagree with me, either, given the manner of their two defeats.

I know I said even the best teams have a few nightmares every season, but you still struggle to fathom how a team this talented could lose by 32 at Charlotte. Only the struggles of other top-10 regulars prevented steeper punishment.
Artest's absence almost makes the Atlanta loss understandable. Almost. Routing Cavs and a road win over Clips couldn't hush the ongoing maturity debate in Indy.
After an impressive, business-like start to their long road trip, Pacers no-showed at Phoenix and finished ragged at Seattle. The good news? Foster is finally back.
Pacers are ''a better team without me,'' Artest says. After a statement like that, and what he added about Carlisle, who can argue with Ron-Ron?

Before you totally dismiss Indy's contender status, don't forget that playing without Artest is not exactly new ground. Pacers have won without him before and still have top-five talent, no matter what they get in a trade.
Artest, at his best, will certainly be missed. But it's not all bleak defensively for Pacers, who are one of only three teams holding opponents under 90 ppg.
You can rationalize road losses to Cavs, Mavs and Spurs. But when Pacers lose at home to Raps, you have to start asking if they're losing focus waiting for a trade.
If you thought last season was one of a kind, think again: Pacers win a couple without O'Neal and Tinsley as the Artest Watch spills into its second month.
Pacers are 10-6 against the West and getting Stephen Jackson's best without Artest: 20-plus points in six of his past seven games -- after just four previously all season.
If it's up to Pacers to lift the city spirits, post-Colts ... uh-oh. They're 9-11 since Artest's trade demand and down to a month left before the deadline to swing a deal.
It figures. Artest finally gets traded and, on cue, Jermaine suffers a long-term injury. Which makes it tough, obviously, to evaluate Peja and JO together.
Just when you think 1-1/2 seasons of adversity had finally flattened these guys, O'Neal-less Pacers stun Detroit to remind everyone that they're still here.
After a season and a half on the Artest roller-coaster, 22 straight days at home give O'Neal-less Pacers a well-deserved chance to steady themselves for once.
What a difference a trade makes. Peja already has four 20-point games in his 5-2 start as a Pacer -- after zero 20-point games in the month of January.
Vince left early with a hamstring tweak, true, but you can't downgrade a road win over tough-at-home Jersey when you remember Pacers don't have O'Neal or Tinsley.
Pacers are 9-5 with Peja, who's averaging 19.6 ppg as a Pacer. So they're not complaining that Artest-for-Maggette fell through, even with Maggette playing again.
When Artest returns Friday, he'll find his old pal Carlisle coming off a bad week . . . but for the most winning no matter how banged-up Pacers are. As usual.
If you subscribe to the Better Off Without Jermaine theory, you should know that Indy is 3-9 in games decided by five points or less since O'Neal last played Jan. 24.
Pacers haven't won two in a row all month, true, but the returns of O'Neal and Tinsley -- and road-heavy Wiz sked -- make Pacers my favorites for the No. 5 spot.
Here's something no one can blame on Artest: Indy is an unforgivable 0-9 against Hawks, Raps and Celts, which is far worse than its current 6-12 slide.
After all they've been through in the past two seasons, now they're crumbling? A 1-7 slide prompts J. O'Neal to say: "We don't even deserve to be in the playoffs."
Bird puts an end to speculation about his coach by saying Carlisle will be back, but the O'Neal trade speculation has only just begun with Pacers dragging to the finish line.

dal.summary: The comeback in Phoenix and the home rout of San Antonio -- as well as the flashes of good D in both -- made more of an impression here than the setback in Utah.
Having played just once at home, and having apparently survived a Dirk back scare without too much panic, Mavs are quietly pleased with where they are so far.
After spanking Spurs and Pistons, Mavs are up here on merit. Not because a procession of locals, including Sam The Locker-Room Attendant, hunted me down Saturday night to lobby for a top-three slot.
As deep as they are, even Mavs are going to be hurting if Howard and Stack are unavailable. Staying up here, then, obviously becomes even more of a challenge.
If teams weren't focusing on him already, this will do it: Nowitzki is averaging 27.8 ppg in Mavs' 11 victories and just 17.8 ppg in the five losses.
Mavs just keep picking up injuries and racking up victories. They've also already beaten just about every team in the league playing well these days.

Avery's first 41 regular-season games in charge produced a 33-8 start -- and this season's launch, on its own, ain't bad, either. Dallas, remember, hasn't played a single game yet with its full squad.
Embarassed as they were by Kobe's 62-pointer, Mavs are 10-1 this month if you throw out that nightmare . . . and Kobe's killer rainbow triple in Dallas on Dec. 12.
Blowing a lead at home to Golden State was uncharacteristically bad. Getting Stack back to deepen a bench that was already deep softens the blow.
No team has consistently hovered on the heels of the Pistons-Spurs duopoly like Mavs, and here's a big reason why: Dallas is 7-1 in the next game after a loss.
Judging by the win margin in Game 1 after the big demotion in Big D -- 33 points over Jersey -- Mavs players were as fed up with Dampier's lethargy as their fans.
The cynic would say Mavs waited too long to sit Dampier. Life was good before the benching, but now look: Dallas is 5-0 since with an average victory margin of 21.
How do you make a run at the Southwest crown and the West's No. 1 seed when you're last in the league in assists? With the league's deepest roster, that's how.
With league's longest active win streak and only three more Ls than Detroit . . . you still won't hear any uproar about Dallas sending only one Mav to the All-Star Game.
The anti-Heat? Dallas is 6-1 in its showdowns with San Antonio, Detroit, Phoenix and Miami, averaging 105.7 ppg and holding those teams to a mere 89.7 ppg.
Since Kobe punked them for 62, Mavs have responded by going 23-4. Since Dampier became a sub, Mavs are 15-1 and have allowed 100 points just once.
Friendly advice: If you want to keep the No. 1 ranking, Dallas, I'd avoid spotting Spurs a lead of 19 or 24, both of which Mavs overcame to beat Grizz and Raps.
Mavs were due for a couple Ls. The greater disappointment is that now, no matter what happened before SA and PHX, they'll be subjected to all the old criticisms.
Avery isn't exactly happy, as everyone knows, but it's not quite panic time yet. Mavs still possess the best record against the rest of the top five at 6-3.
How deep is that Mavs bench? So deep that Nellie steps down and, exactly one year later, they've got a top Coach of the Year contender in his place.
Mavs might be 1-2 against hated Spurs, but they'll be 6-1 vs. the rest of the top five if they can pull a Utah and sweep the season series from Detroit on Tuesday.
Van Horn's broken hand means he's likely lost for the year. A 10-8 malaise means No. 1 in the West is looking all but lost as well for banged-up Mavs.
Mavs followed up the worst week of their season (three straight Ls) with perhaps their best, led by Nowitzki going for 59 points combined against Artest and Bowen.
Mavs probably have to win the West for Nowitzki to be MVP. But to win in the playoffs, Dallas' key might be Josh Howard, since Mavs are 19-0 when he scores at least 20.

mil.summary: Bucks have to be Team O' The Week, with a couple candidates for Player O' The Week (Redd and T.J. Ford). Bogut's week wasn't bad, either, was it?
Not trying to put a damper on the heady start, but now we'll really assess Bucks' progress with four games out West ... and only seven road wins last season.
With two lopsided losses sandwiched around a nice win at GS, Bucks need to beat a beat-up Utah in the trip's finale to add credence to their promising start.

Heartwarming as Ford's comeback is, all the glowing coverage he's getting doesn't mean Bucks can get away with the defense they've been playing. Only four teams are giving up more than Milwaukee's 99.7 ppg allowed.
Folks have been excited about Bucks' depth ever since the Magloire deal, but the focus was on the frontcourt. They seem even deeper than expected now that Mo Williams keeps tossing in game-winners.
Joe Smith's knee injury could have been a serious setback. But Bogut has looked rather NBA-ready, hasn't he? So it's not.

Bucks would be more inclined to celebrate the fact that they've already matched last season's seven road wins if they hadn't lost both home games last week with some uncharacteristically frigid 3-point shooting (6 for 36).
This is what you call livin' right: Bucks are 11-2 against the East, 13-1 when they score 100 points or more and 9-0 in games decided by five points or less.
Routed in Orlando ... and they lose T.J., too? The committee (of one) actually does feel a bit guilty after making such a fuss about how Bucks have been livin' right.
T.J. Ford does everything fast, apparently. And no one's happier to see him back so soon than Redd, who shot 36 percent from the floor in four-plus games without him.
It's gotten to the (worrying) point that Bucks are winning only the close ones. They're up to 9-0 in games decided by three points or fewer, but mired in a 4-7 funk overall.
How does a team get over its first loss in a tight game? In Bucks' case, games against Hawks and Bobcats couldn't have come at a better time.
Bucks have been over .500 every day since Nov. 29. Of course, they also seem to be dealing with a new injury every day. This time it's Mo Williams . . . again.
With competition like Rip, Vince, Pierce, Arenas and Kidd, it'll probably be easier for Redd to get Milwaukee to the playoffs than get himself to Houston.
Class act that he is, Redd is taking his All-Star snub better than I am, quietly keeping banged-up Milwaukee above .500 for the fourth successive month.
Time to solidify their playoff position? Banged-up Bucks reconvened after the All-Star break with a full complement of players for the first time all season.
Bucks are still 11-5 in games decided by three points or less or overtime, but they're also looking increasingly shaky at 11-17 since that 17-11 start.
As if a dwindling lead over No. 9 Bulls and a home loss to Knicks aren't enough, there's this for sub-.500 Bucks: Magloire just took a swipe at Stotts' rotation.
If they want to at least hang on to the eighth slot, this has to stop: Bucks have lost five straight home games to grease their 3-7 slide since the All-Star break.
It's been a rocky month, but surviving an Atlanta scare and then thumping No. 9 Bulls seem to have steadied things after those slippage fears.
With T.J. Ford and Mo Williams still banged up and just three games left against non-playoff teams, Bucks will be fortunate to still be a .500 team at season's end.
Turning that 15-zip start at Detroit into a win would have made it Bucks' best week of the season. But it was still pretty good, with wins over Suns and Pacers.
Only in the East: Bucks suddenly need to run the table (5-0) if they want to finish above .500 ... but might wind up with the No. 6 seed regardless.
Sen. Kohl has said he expects Bucks to finish no lower than sixth in the East and, amazingly, they still have a shot at sixth (or fifth) despite a 23-30 record since Jan. 1.

phx.summary: Amare-less Suns have just started a five-game homestand ... but perhaps that's not such great news after the torturous manner of their losses to Dallas and Sacto.

Amare-less Suns needed a pick-me-up after three late collapses at home, and here it is: Diaw and Barbosa are contributing faster than anyone envisioned, which certainly can't hurt the long-term outlook.
When will the darkness lift? The brightest spot in a bleak start -- Barbosa -- is suddenly out 2-3 weeks with a knee sprain suffered in a narrow loss to Spurs.
When they needed it most, Suns presented with three foes in worse funks than theirs: Raps, Rockets and Nets. It looks like they've restored a bit of confidence.

The schedule has been undeniably kind lately, but Suns aren't getting enough credit for their recent stingy D (a mere 90.5 ppg allowed in this 7-1 stretch) and the help Nash and Matrix are getting from a slew of newcomers.

Remember when D'Antoni said in the weekend edition of the Daily Dime that Amare-less Suns would win 50 because Nash ''has always won 50'' and would figure things out?  Not such an outlandish claim anymore, is it?
The plan to counter Joe Johnson's departure was amassing depth. But when you add a few new injuries to the Amare situation, Suns don't have depth anymore, either.

Tantalizing as it is to hear Amare is recovering nicely, Suns would settle first for getting Barbosa healthy. They're 2-4 since the little Brazilian reinjured his knee and also lost the game (Clips) in which he went down.
Best of both worlds: Amare is traveling with the team again ... and Suns are 4-0 on a five-game trip to make it clear that there's no need for him to rush back.
Why didn't they think of this sooner? Formal name change from America West Arena to US Airways Center coincides with back-to-back sweep of Heat and then Spurs.
If you want to beat these guys these days, take them to triple overtime. Suns' only two losses in the past 11 games came in three OTs (Knicks and Nuggets).
Check that. If you want to beat these guys, taking them to double overtime works, too. Seattle didn't need a third to heap more OT misery on Suns.
Good as they are sans Amare, Suns have to fix this with or without him: 0-5 in games decided by three points or less, thanks in part to all those OT heartbreakers.
As valuable as Nash is -- again -- try not to ignore Marion. This is also the best Matrix we've ever seen, even if he continues to be underrated and taken for granted.
For all their success sans Amare, Suns aren't celebrating yet, knowing they don't have enough separation from Clips to believe they've sewn up a top-three seed.
No joke: I think Suns can get to the Finals even without Stoudemire, assuming they get all the way to the West finals and let Mavs and Spurs beat each other up first.
GM and owner are on the outs and K. Thomas is suddenly out up to two months, but Suns needn't fret too much yet with a six-game lead in the Pacific.
I had the wrong Frenchman at Most Improved Player in my Weekend Dime. It should be Diaw, now a nightly triple-double threat at center, over Parker.
Didn't see that one coming, frankly: Sunday's setback in Portland was just Suns' second loss since Feb. 1 with Nash on the floor.
Even at their hottest, these Suns struggle to keep up with Spurs. Of course, they had that same problem with a better-than-ever Stoudemire in the playoffs.
Quirk of the Week: First three foes in Amare's comeback each have their own big-name microfracture patient -- Randolph (Blazers), K-Mart (Nuggets), Kidd (Nets).
Suns are just 7-7 since that 11-game win streak. But it's not as if they're going to panic now, remembering how they recovered from a 4-5 start.
Make that 8-9 since the 11-game win streak, but it's not all bleak: There's no 50-win team in Suns' way until the West finals. They won't see pesky Sonics again, either.
This has to be worth a couple COY votes in itself: D'Antoni, don't forget, guaranteed 50 wins after Amare went down ... and again after Suns' 4-5 start.

bkn.summary: J-Kidd, RJ and Vinsanity, according to Kidd, are a modern-day Run TMC. Maybe so, but after all the good press lately, losing to Milwaukee was a jolt.
Houston can probably justify a sub-.500 record, having lost T-Mac briefly. Nets have a bit more explaining to do, tough sked or not.
Vince has been held under 20 in four straight games. J-Kidd has topped six assists only four times. Not stuff you want to hear entering a five-game trip out West.

Our buddy Sanford, ace ESPN researcher and World's Biggest Nets Fan, says the biggest problem is actually the new play-by-play guy. He concedes that Marv is a legend, but Sanford says no one can replace ''a true Net'' like Ian Eagle.
Best thing you can say about Jersey is that Houston still has a longer list of problems. Otherwise Nets would be the league's most disappointing team.
The committee (of one) reserves the right to update its thinking, and we did: Nets are far from fixed, but Wiz still edge them as East's main disappointment to date.

Maybe, just maybe, wins over Nuggets and Warriors suggest Nets finally realize that the season has started. Of course, just before those victories, Jersey lost at home to Charlotte and by 20 to Arenas-less Wiz.
He's not going to score 51 every time, but Vince -- averaging 35.4 ppg in this 5-0 spurt -- has to keep playing this way for Nets to offset their size and bench issues.

Happy New Year? The league's hottest team -- no one has an active win streak close to this eight-gamer -- would be even happier if it didn't have to wait until Friday for its next game. A scheduling quirk means a full week off to interrupt Nets' flow.
The week off figured to help preserve Nets' hold on the coveted No. 4 slot. But they barely held on, even after Vince's buzzer-beater in Toronto. Suns are that hot.
Three straight losses to bring a thudding end to their hot streak, all without Jefferson, reconfirm that two out of three of their stars ain't enough for Nets.
Just for fun, let's assume Nets beat Heat out for the No. 2 seed and home-court advantage in Round 2. Would you still pick Miami to win that series?
Losing Vince is obviously the killer blow, but this hurts, too: Nets no longer have the league's longest win streak of the season now that Pistons have won 11 straight.
It really would have been a special week had they won in Cleveland, too, but quality wins over Pistons and Heat stretch Nets' home unbeaten streak to 10.
If you have to bid farewell to a 12-game home winning streak, you can accept it a little easier when the hottest team in the league is the one that halts it. Maybe.
My favorite Nets fan, Sanford, is livid about Kidd's All-Star snub, with Jersey leading its division, but I bet Kidd benefits from a weekend off as much as anyone.
Heat have a cushy stretch-run schedule, but Nets had the second-easiest coming out of the break based on opponent win PCT: .467 to Miami's .446.
It might have been a bit premature to suggest in the Midweek Dime that Nets had cemented their top-six standing. They haven't, even with Kidd playing great.
If Artest trade rumors are really what got Vince rolling back in December, it might be time for Nets -- mired in a 2-5 funk -- to spread some new ones.
That's five wins on the trot, after a run of four losses in five games, after reeling off four consecutive wins. The word, I believe, is streaky.
Frank wants folks to stop talking so much about his Big Three, but let's face it: Nets don't stay up here unless we're talking about Vince, Kidd and R.J. A lot.
Just a hunch: If Nets keep holding teams to 81 ppg, as they have been during their 12-game unbeaten run, this is going to wind up being bigger than a hot streak.
It's tough to see Nets making up 2 1/2 games on Miami with a week and change to go. Then again, who expected Nets to go 15-1 and get this close?
Fifty wins is a big deal to these guys, especially after a 9-12 start, but Nets seem to be picking up bandwagon support for the Miami series either way.

was.summary: Don't get carried away even with this jump. A 3-0 start is a 3-0 start, but Wiz haven't racked up many strength-of-schedule points yet in beating Raps, Knicks and Magic.
Arenas can be rather amazing, but you already knew that. Maybe the best part about Washington's start is its league-leading opponent FG defense: 39.1 percent.

You know by now that we dispute the existence of a Power Rankings jinx. Wiz fans, though, will be pardoned for their jinx e-mails after being forced to toast their historic rise to No. 3 with three straight road defeats.

After spanking Spurs and thinking they've arrived, Wiz lost five straight. Then Wiz got routed by Charlotte after winning at Detroit, making me wonder if they've learned yet that the season isn't over after you've beaten a powerhouse.

Wiz have already blown their gift opportunity to gain some early Southeast ground on Shaq-less Miami. And they know it. ''Hopefully this will be our worst month of the season,'' Coach Jordan said of a 7-7 November.

Sad but true: More than anyone else in the East, Wiz have left me wanting more. They've teased us twice -- looking so good vs. Spurs and Pistons -- but more regularly have fallen shy of their potential . . . even without the departed Hughes.
Halting this slump is more than a one-step process, but forbidding Arenas from scoring fewer than 20 is a good place to start. When that happens, Wiz are 0-6.
Wiz have made a habit of winning the games you least expect. Add their victories in Denver and Phoenix to the list, after Wiz slipped five games under .500.
Wiz are 3-2 since Butler became a starter. That said, Wiz were 3-0 with Butler as a starter before surrendering 232 points in home losses to Phoenix and Miami.
Just like their first-round playoff foes from Chicago, Wiz are five games under .500. The difference? One coach (Jordan) is feeling more heat than the other (Skiles).
The lineup shakeup of the under-fire Jordan seems to be working. But before anyone gets too carried away, remember that two of those three wins came against Atlanta.
Like Toronto's Mitchell and Atlanta's Woodson, Wiz coach Jordan manufactures a winning run -- 6-3 since an embarrassing rout at NY -- when he needs it most.
Jamison is looking more like Jamison, having strung together eight straight 20-plus games after his recent benching. Wiz, though, remain a difficult read.
Even after a 10-5 uptick, Wiz haven't seen .500 since Dec. 6. The good news? Only two teams (Bulls, Magic) are realistically chasing them for the No. 8 spot.
Red-hot Wiz love that Le Commish put Arenas in the AS Game. But they didn't mind the snubbed Arenas who went for 45 after finding out the coaches didn't pick him.
At least one problem solved: Arenas and rest of Wiz won't be pining for Hughes in the second half, knowing that Cavs won't have him, either.
Arenas is on record as saying he thinks Wiz will finish fifth in the East. But fourth is not out of the question, even though No. 6 is really the best seed of the three.
Here's a rare Wiz stat that doesn't involve Gilbert Arenas: Washington's recent nine-game home winning streak was its longest since a 15-gamer in (yikes) 1989.
Wiz are the one East team that can honestly say they'd be better off seeing Detroit than Miami in the playoffs. Wiz have now beaten Pistons twice and never beat Heat.
No one else in the East's top eight has fewer road wins than No. 5 Washington's 10. Something to keep in mind with Wiz playing 12 of their final 17 games away.
Do Butler and Daniels (combined) replace Hughes? The standings say it's close: Wiz are only three games worse than their 38-30 record at this stage last season.
Wiz couldn't quite pull off a season sweep of Spurs, but a 3-3 trip out West -- painful as the last two games were -- keeps them in the lead for the No. 5 seed.
Still got it: As soon as I labeled Wiz as the East's most credible lower-seeded team, three key players -- Butler, Daniels and (yikes) Arenas -- all get dinged up.
Back-to-back playoff berths for the first time since 1988 is nice. Winning one more game to ensure that the East won't have four sub-.500 playoff teams is better.

mia.summary: The only solace for SVG with Shaq out is that the coach can't be under the microscope when one of the two franchise players is injured. Can he?

Even 'Toine and J-Will should be able to agree that now is the time to rack up some wins without Shaq. Miami's eight opponents for the rest of the month include Hornets, Raps, Blazers, Magic, Knicks and Hawks.
Heat's 5-3 record sans Shaq ain't bad. Heat's crunch-time collapse Sunday in Toronto was criminal, Shaq or no Shaq.
The one thing I liked about Miami's roster composition is the idea that all these big names could carry Heat through Shaq's absence. But even that's not happening now.
Maybe it's just me, Heat faithful. But even with Shaq out, I expect more than three road wins so far. Before this week, Miami hadn't won away since Opening Night.
We knew Heat, as soon as Shaq got back, would be starting over on their ambitious chemistry project. But they're actually starting all the way over, with Riles back as well.
If nothing else, Riles has a division title in his future. Heat's effort was so much better in his first four games that the Southeast is pretty much clinched already.
After all the Christmas Day hoopla, Heat are 5-2 and averaging 102.1 ppg under Riley. But bigger tests come this week against Bucks (home) and Pistons (road).

On one hand, Heat can take encouragement from their showing in Detroit, given how early it is in Riley's second reign. On the other hand, Pistons never really looked like they were going to lose that one. Did they?
If Riles' goal was shifting the focus off Wade missing a game and an ugly start to a seven-game trip, dropping hints about leaving coaching at season's end did the trick.
With the focus on Artest, Francis and Pistons v. Spurs/Kobe v. LeBron, Heat quietly assembled their best week all season, capped by the win at red-hot Utah.
It was Riley, not me, who called Miami a ''41-game disappointment.'' But the ''new'' East is so disappointing that Heat probably snare the No. 2 seed no matter what.
Don't blame the committee (of one messenger). Facts is facts: Heat are 16-8 under Riles, but 0-6 against the top four and just 8-13 vs. teams with winning records.
With Shaq back in Jersey, and Heat (seemingly) rolling at last, figured we'd see something big from the big guy. Try 11 points/six TOs vs. Collins and Uncle Cliffy.
It's about time you brought some heat, Heat. Now to see if you turn Sunday into a real turning point or if it makes you even more lax for the rest of the regular season.
Between now and April 1, Heat have only four games (out of 18) against teams with winning records. Let's see whether they can stay serious when the schedule is soft.
Shaq's belief, borrowed from Phil Jackson, is that only the last 30 games matter. Not a philosophy Riles shares, but Shaq does seem to be turning up the intensity.
Can't overhype this win streak with Heat fed seven straight cupcakes after the Detroit breakthrough. But we don't want to be too downbeat on Shaq's 34th birthday.
Heat have two cracks left at Detroit to improve this ledger: Miami remains 1-7 against the rest of the top five, with Detroit at 4-2, Spurs at  6-4 and Suns at 4-6.
Why haven't Heat, now 13-1 since beating Detroit on Feb. 12, been promoted? They can't crack top four having only played two over-.500 teams (Cavs, Wiz) in that span.
Heat don't need 'Zo to clinch the No. 2 seed. They really don't even need him before the second round. But they do need 'Zo to go toe-to-toe with Pistons.
Thursday vs. Detroit is Heat's last chance to wow us before the playoffs. Sunday's loss to Nets dropped Miami to 2-11 against the committee's top five.
Seriously: Since Miami's playoff fantasies depend on a dose of Old School Shaq against Detroit, maybe it's safest to just park The Diesel for the final five games.
If I pointed out that the Fla. team to beat Cavs, Mavs, Pistons and Spurs since March 10 wasn't Miami, would you call me a truth teller or Heat Hater? Right. Heat Hater it is.

lal.summary: What does Smush have in common with Kareem, Wilkes, Ceballos and Shaq? True story: They're the only five Lakers ever to score at least 20 in their first two games with the team, which includes the Minneapolis/Mikan days.
The big Hollywood showdown this week? No, not Phil vs. Larry on Wednesday. Try Lakers vs. Clips on Friday.
Reality is starting to set in for Kobe and Phil. Kwame's out at least two weeks, and Smush is averaging just 8.0 ppg over the past six on 31.5 percent shooting.
Sunday night's thriller vs. Nets aside, Lakers have been hard on the eyes. Kobe needs 29 shots a game to average 34.1 ppg, and no other Laker averages 15 ppg.

Weird week. Lakers blew a game they should have won (vs. Minny) and stole two they should have lost (at Utah, vs. Charlotte). L.A.'s next six games, meanwhile, are all roadies, which makes me think Kobe isn't going to stop shooting.
Even if the Zenmeister has gone over the line with his Kwame cracks, that's about all you can find fault with. To have this crew at .500, through 20 games, is something.
They don't call him Zenmeister (OK, I don't) for nothing. But even Phil would tell you that he never expected these Lakers, this soon, to reel off a 7-2 run.
Whatever happens in the last two games of '05, Lakers will gladly take a 10-win December, given November's woes (5-8) and with only six home games this month.
It wasn't so long ago that December seemed like such a joyous month in Lakerland. Now? L.A. could be under .500 by the time Kobe is back from his two-game cooldown.
Maybe Phil won't have to deal directly with Kobe's fury. Maybe the suspension did it for him, judging by the 98 points of anger No. 8 unleashed on Sixers and Clips.
Kobe's critics have quieted down because now he's racking up wins, too. But why should he shoot less when Lakers are 0-7 when Odom takes 15 or more shots?
Even before Kobe's 81, Zenmeister wasn't lowering expectations. Says Phil, regarding Artest: ''We're like a player away from really stepping into another level.''
If you say Kobe doesn't make his teammates better, what you're really saying is that you expected these Lakers to be more than a top-10 team. These Lakers?
Odom can't be all bad, can he? Without him, Lakers suffer two lopsided losses (in Charlotte and OKC) to bring a hasty halt to the Kobe 4 MVP talk.
The schedule should help Lakers from here: 20 of their final 32 games are at home. Of course, at 1-5 in February, it suddenly looks like Kobe needs a lot of help.
This is a big reason Lakers spent so much money to get Phil back: Zenmeister teams are 14-for-14 all-time when it comes to making the playoffs.
January: Kobe averaged 43.4 ppg in 13 games; LA went 9-4. February: Kobe's at 31.8 ppg; LA is 4-8. Conclusion: Kobe needs to start shooting more.
Even after beating Pistons, Lakers have to be careful. They were also 31-29 last season after a big win over Dallas . . . and won three more games all season.
The good news? Lakers have been .500 or better every day since Jan. 6. The bad news? Wins over Detroit and San Antonio inside a week didn't intimidate Seattle.
Even with Kobe and Phil, you can't expect more than a seventh or eighth seed for Lakers. But if they slip, they get relegated to my Most Disappointing Teams list.
Of course Kobe is playing too many minutes. But it's not as though (A) Lakers have other alternatives or (B) their playoff spot is slipping away.
What a difference a Zenmeister makes? Last season's Lakers went 8-24 after the All-Star break. These Lakers are 14-9 and sure to finish over .500 now.
Zenmeister Jackson had never experienced a season with more than 35 losses before this season ... but even Kobe says it's Phil's best coaching job ever.
Not even those of us who did pick Lakers to make the playoffs saw this coming: Clips are the city champs again, but Lakers have reduced the gap to almost nil.

lac.summary: How many guesses would you need to identify the only team in the West that hasn't lost yet? A few, I'm guessing, before you went with Clips.
How many guesses would you need to identify the only team in the league to beat Wiz? A few, I'm guessing, before you went with those still-hot Clips.
There's no shortage of skeptics saying this can't last, and maybe they're right. Or maybe this is the playoff year Mr. Brand, one of the good guys, has long deserved.
Dunleavy himself warned Clips not to get carried away, noting their comfy schedule so far. In other words, No. 4 might have been a touch too high.

Clips haven't reached double figures in victories this fast since 1977-78, when the franchise broke my heart by making that the final season in Buffalo. I moved to SoCal with 'em, but the relationship ended at the Aud.
Beating a hot team like Suns, without Maggette, moves Clips ''up another notch'' in Dunleavy's estimation. If you disagree, you're in a dwindling minority.
Perhaps the honeymoon isn't all the way over. Clips just beat hot Houston, welcomed Livingston back from injury and still -- still! -- cling to first place in the Pacific.
OK. After five straight road defeats, plus the news that Maggette is out at least four more weeks, it appears that the honeymoon period is indeed history.
Yup. Starting a comfy stretch (nine of 11 at home) with two heavy defeats to sub-.500 teams (Kings and Celts) means the honeymoon period is definitely gonzo.
Tough for Clips, in the midst of a 3-9 funk, to get too excited about Kaman's surge when the timetable for Maggette's return keeps getting stretched and stretched.
As if the evaporation of their darling status wasn't sufficiently problematic, Clips (mainly their coach) have to mend fences with Maggette after the near-trade to Indy.
Clips are a passable 4-2 since dropping within three games of .500. Tough, though, to get noticed in L.A. when Kobe's going for 50-something every other game.
They couldn't get Artest, don't know when Maggette will be back and can't get any pub thanks to Kobe. The consolation? Clips are back up to nine games over .500.
Over .500 in February for just the fifth time in 36 seasons doesn't make this the best team in club history yet. My beloved Braves, don't forget, started 33-17 in '74-75.
Sam I Am was snubbed so completely that almost no one even mentions him as a snubbee. And Clips might just deserve two All-Stars given how well they've done.
The reward for being the best Clips ever? Mavs or Spurs in the first round unless they either pass Suns with all these moves they're making ... or drop a slot or two.
This is a recording: This is the best team in Los Angeles, even when Clips take a five-game losing streak into a Staples showdown with downtrodden Lakers.
A 3-7 slump should be alarming, especially after Clips trade for Radmanovic and regain Maggette, but let's be honest. Finishing sixth in the West is better anyway.
Yet one more reason to take new Clips seriously: This is a 15-15 road team. Clips haven't won 15 on the road since going 15-26 in 1996-97 . . . their last playoff team.
It's not a question anyone was asking in October, but you have to ask it now: Can Clips actually win 50? My beloved Braves, I hate to admit, never won more than 49.
OK, OK. Fifty wins, requiring a 9-4 finish, is probably pushing it. But even 40 wins is something in Clipperdom, where it hadn't happened for 12 seasons.
Only 10 games left, but we'll see Clips in potential playoff previews against both teams -- Denver once and Dallas twice -- they can be matched up with in Round 1.
Clips need a 6-0 finish for the best record in franchise history. I'm guessing they'd settle for a healthier and happier Maggette. Mobley, too.
After Clips' 16-point home loss to Seattle, Tuesday's much-discussed showdown in Memphis might not even matter. No. 6 is just about theirs.

mem.summary: Suggested SportsNation poll: Which is the uglier look -- Pau's scraggly beard or the sight of Battier with a nasty head wound?
Turns out Grizz fans apparently like Pau's beard. They also seem to like Pau's aggression so far, apart from a muted showing in Boston in a frustrating one-point L.
Grizz need only one more win this month to set a franchise record for November victories. So, yes, addition by subtraction is working so far.

OK, granted, No. 4 might be tough to justify. But this has become the toughest slot to fill each week, thanks to the struggles of various would-be elite teams, and Grizz just went to Dallas and won by 20 without two regulars (Miller and Cardinal).
No one seems to think they can stay up here. Of course, if Grizz keep holding foes to 85.5 points per game -- easily tops in the league -- we might have to reevaluate.
After their two previous two-game losing streaks, Grizz reeled off win streaks of four and six games, respectively. This time ... let's see.
During the recent three-game skid, with Pau in a funk, Grizz averaged only 76 ppg. Even with their stingy defense, you've got to score at least 86.
Make that two impressive team stats: Grizz are off to a 10-4 start against fellow West foes to go with a defense that's still holding the opposition under 86 ppg.
That elbow Miller took from Kobe can't compare to these painful realities: Damon is lost for the season and Bobby Jax (hamstring) missed eight games in December.
My apologies. Grizz have played as though they don't realize Stoudamire's injury is supposed to drop them a notch or two. Until they got to Chicago, anyway.
Not sure if it's Kobe's elbow or trade rumors, but Miller has been sparked into some monster numbers lately for a Grizz group on pace to win a whopping 54.
It'll be interesting to see how Grizz deal with their first crisis of the season. Not that slipping to sixth (and out of the SA-DAL bracket) would be so bad for them.
This is not the way to make an All-Star push: Grizz have dropped seven of nine and, fair or not, I suspect that'll put a dent in Pau's hopes for a spot in Houston.
No slight to Pau and Co., but Grizz really aren't top-five material. And this comes, remember, from someone who liked them in the preseason more than most.
We've seen some defensive slippage, but Grizz are still one of three teams holding foes under 90 ppg. That's why I doubt Grizz will slip much further.
Grizz return to work with the NBA's stingiest defense (87.7 ppg) and the first All-Star in club history (Pau). That's why they're giddier than your typical No. 7 seed.
With that D we're always raving about, you'd think Grizz wouldn't blow two double-digit leads (even to Mavs and Spurs) and then lose to Wolves after KG gets tossed.
After dropping 13 of 18 in one stretch, worst appears to be over for Grizz. At least Jerry West thinks so, because The Logo apparently has guaranteed a playoff berth.
Still clinging to that favorable No. 6 seed and still looking pretty stingy: Grizz have allowed 100 or more just 10 times all season, two of those being OT games.
If you had forgotten about Big Jake before this month's hot streak, don't fret. Grizz didn't even remember to put him on the playoff roster last spring.
Since apparently no one was injured in Sunday's elevator fire in their building, I guess we're safe pointing out that Grizz are suddenly the hottest team in the West.
Want more evidence that there's more to Pau's game than ever? The bearded Spaniard averaged almost six assists a game in March.
Five games left. Four against sub-.500 squads and the fifth is at home against Clips. In other words, No. 5 in the West is there for the taking. If Grizz want it, that is.
A note about that No. 5 seed supposedly no one in the West wants: Grizz are 6-1 in April, which is pretty much the antithesis of tanking.

uta.summary: AK-47 is filling up box scores again and the rookie Williams looks OK, but Boozer's ongoing absence slices into the optimism somewhat.
AK-47's ankle injury doesn't appear to be serious. Yet it's serious enough to remind you what happened to Utah when he got hurt early last season.

Sloan had never endured a season in Utah like last season ... and, unbelievably, this season is shaping up to be a similar story.  Outlook has changed drastically with Boozer (hamstring) and Kirilenko (ankle) possibly out a month (or more) each.

I'd like to think that last week's steep demotion was just the spark injury-hit Utah needed. I suppose, however, that Kirilenko's earlier-than-expected return this week will probably have a bigger impact.
Can't decide what's more shocking: Utah getting jobbed on a late call at home ... or Utah, even with all the injuries, sporting a 2-6 record at the Delta Center.
Out on a limb we go: If Kirilenko can't shake his funk and Boozer never comes back, it won't matter that Okur is playing the best ball of his life.
Kirilenko is back and rounding into some rhythm, but is the key to success actually Okur? When Memo leads Jazz in scoring and rebounding, they're 5-2.
You hear Kirilenko is ailing anew and you see Boozer miss another CLE trip and you inevitably wonder if this felt more like Groundhog Day than Christmas in the SLC.

On second thought, maybe life is starting to brighten for the only team out there that can claim victories over Detroit and Dallas. After all, Jazz are 13-8 when Kirilenko is healthy, as he is now ... compared to just 2-8 without him.
When you've got Milt Palacio, who needs John Stockton? An exaggeration, perhaps, but for one magical overtime in Motown, you couldn't laugh at that question.
The way Jazz are flowing, on an 8-1 run until Saturday's home setback to Miami, perhaps it's better that Boozer needs more time before making his comeback.
Uh-oh. After all the fuss over their record with (17-8) and without (2-8) their star, Jazz go on to drop four of five with no Kirilenko injury to blame it on.
Uh-oh, continued: Utah's slide is now at 2-6 and Jazz have two point guards (McLeod and Palacio) looking steadier than No. 3 pick Williams.
If we're going to keep zinging Atlanta for passing on CP3 (and we probably are) Jazz have to get it, too, for drafting a struggling Williams (Deron) of their own.
If you're thinking (hoping?) Boozer is being showcased, think again. He missed almost a year, so Jazz couldn't trade him before the deadline if they wanted to.
Boozer is finally back to help Kirilenko and Okur, but Jazz have to be wondering whether they were too hasty in parting with Mo Williams and a surging Kirk Snyder.
First Jazz go to OKC and give their playoff push a boost by beating Hornets in first of four stretch-run meetings. Then Jazz turn around and lose to NO/OKC in SLC.
I just don't know if this Jazz ever will be healthy enough to make a lasting playoff push. What I do know is that Kirilenko is the talk of the league.
Focus, if you wish, on the umpteenth Larry Miller rant. We won't, because (1) Sloan was never really in trouble, and (2) we're not ready to put the AK-47 story to bed.
After four losses in five games -- and after five Jazz starters combined for a meager 26 points against Miami -- this is no time for Kirilenko jokes.
Mailman's retirement ceremony, with his little buddy Stockton on hand, didn't exactly inspire the next generation. This Jazz crew has dropped below .500 at home, at 17-18.
AK-47 found a good way to get us to stop talking about his spouse, averaging five blocks in the past seven games to go with 18.9 ppg, 10.3 rpg and 4.6 apg.
Jazz are 7-5 with their new lineup, which doesn't make the playoffs realistic, but it does mean Kirilenko is technically blocking all these shots as a shooting guard now.
Boozer is so hot and Jazz got so close that Utahns probably can't help it. It's only natural to wish Utah gambled to bring him back a little sooner.

den.summary: Interim coach Scotty Brooks said it best: After a nightmare start, Nuggets already need an ''early-season turnaround'' from rally specialist Furious George.
Camby is playing better-than-ever ball. Of course, if Nuggets don't have Nene or K-Mart, Camby might have to go for 18, 22 and seven every night.
Stat we didn't see coming: Nuggets are 4-0 this season when K-Mart sits, after going 10-2 without him last season. With K-Mart? Just 41-36 overall.

Furious George, remember, told us two weeks ago that ''we're not that far away from being a good team.'' This subsequent 5-1 run is more like it ... as long as Camby, fresh off receiving our praise, was really out for only one game.

Nuggets have more losses through 18 games than Furious George suffered in 40 games last season. And, yes, even the four losses under poor Scotty Brooks -- the only UC Irvine guy I've ever been able to tolerate -- do count on Karl's record.
The 3-point shooting is still amiss -- 24.9 percent as a team -- but 'Melo's 40-point night in Miami suggest that Nuggets' misfortune with injuries might finally be fading.
Come to think of it, with K-Mart hobbling and 'Melo's scoring unable to prevent a sub-.500 record, Nugs actually aren't far away from desperate. Which only further explains their Artest interest.
Yes: Nuggets still want Artest and continue to look for consistency that extends beyond Camby and 'Melo. No: Nuggets don't appear close to either one yet.
Maybe the plan is sinking all the way to 17-25, like last season, and then surging to 32-8 finish that makes Furious George look like twice the genius.
Anyone else out there expecting Melo, who averaged 29.3 ppg in December, to get more All-Star support from the West's coaches than Grizzlies' Gasol?
It might not be enough to get him to the All-Star Game in a crowded West frontcourt, but 'Melo's ongoing surge has Camby-less Nuggets at a healthy 5-2 in 2006.
On second thought, this month's 9-2 record -- all without Camby -- might indeed be enough to make 'Melo an All-Star. Even in the West, are there five better Fs?
I agree with Denver's belief that working Camby back in shouldn't be that tough. But his first two games (home-and-home losses to Clips) couldn't have been worse.
Yes: 'Melo and Stevie Francis both have MD ties. But no: The idea of making them teammates (Furious George's idea, I'm told) holds no appeal at all to me.
No team has endured trade-rumor uncertainty longer than Nugs, but putting the first blemish on Dallas' perfect month might be what revives K-Mart and Co.
I don't see any 25-4 runs in their immediate future, but I'd bank on a big finish from a motivated 'Melo ... if rumor-weary Nuggets can regroup after the deadline.
I keep hearing that Denver was supposed to get a shooter at the deadline, but who was available? Evans (rebounding) and Patterson (perimeter D) fill voids, too.
With a seven-game trip looming, Nuggets appear to be at their up-and-down best, following up a home spanking from Bucks by punishing Pistons.
A proven perimeter shooter would be nice. But what Denver might need just as much is more nail-biters: Nuggets are 13-2 in their last 15 one-point games.
Nuggets haven't quite matched their 25-4 form from last season's roaring finish, but this 10-4 spurt -- which includes a 5-2 road trip -- has all but clinched a No. 3 seed.
Thanks to a 26-14 mark since Jan. 1, Nuggets' 14-17 start is a memory. One more month like March (10-4) and the West's No. 6 seed won't look so enticing, either.
The bad news? Nuggets are just 4-8 against the West's top three. The good news: They're also on the verge of the franchise's first division title since (gasp) 1988.
K-Mart. Boykins. And now Najera. It's a good thing 'Melo's getting so good (30.5 ppg in his last 14 games) because Nuggets' injury bug is as consistent as he is.
If we're going to laud Nuggets for claiming their first division title since 1988, I suppose we do have to mention that it's a six-division league now as opposed to four.

hou.summary: If Denver's outlook has changed, how about Houston's? Rockets won't be doing any playoff damage if T-Mac doesn't shake these back and knee woes.
JVG was lamenting his team's lack of speed before they went out and lost to Boston by 20. Don't know how fast Spree is at 35, but it's probably worth checking out.
Rockets know they can recover because they overturned a 6-11 start last season. Of course, T-Mac wasn't ailing then like he is now.
Problems, indeed. T-Mac's out, Houston hasn't won a home game since Opening Night, no one has a longer losing streak (seven) and only Toronto has more losses.

Rockets are only 4-4 when T-Mac plays, but there's no disputing what he does for his center. Yao is shooting 60.4 percent from the field when T-Mac is out there and a disconcerting 40.6 percent when he's not.
Can't even say for sure that this is the Team O' The Week From Texas, after Mavs went 4-0. But a 3-0 week, given how punchless Rockets have looked, is a big boost.
Apparently that detour to Vegas changed Rockets' luck only to a degree. Yao going down indefinitely means their injury luck hasn't changed a whole lot.

After winning six one-point games last season, Rockets knew their luck might change. But not this drastically. With Yao out now, T-Mac forced to play hurt and a few more injuries, they've zoomed past unlucky all the way to tortured.
Remember all those nasty things folks said about Yao when Rockets went 0-8 with T-Mac out? It's getting closer to apology time: Houston is just 1-5 when Yao is hurt.
No Yao and no T-Mac? Good thing Houston will be hosting the All-Star Game, because it suddenly has no All-Stars in this bad-to-worse nightmare of a season.
It doesn't show in the standings, with Rockets now 0-13 in games McGrady misses or can't finish, but Juwan has averaged a game 25 and 12 since T-Mac's latest setback.
This has become something bigger than a problem. Houston hasn't won a home game since Dec. 6, which shouldn't happen even without T-Mac.
Assuming Yao is back soon, and assuming T-Mac doesn't immediately reinjure his back, you still have to wonder about Yao's stamina after he sat for so long.
Why do Rockets believe they can still leapfrog seven or eight teams to make the playoffs. They're 12-6 when T-Mac and Yao are healthy and, for now, both are.
Problems? To leapfrog five teams into the playoffs, Houston must keep improving that 8-16 home record. And March is the time to do it, with 11 of 15 games at home.
The skeptic in me says that, even though Rockets are still mathematically in the playoff hunt, A-S weekend will prove to be the peak of T-Mac's nightmare season.
One more problem for Houston to contend with: No team returned to work last Tuesday with a tougher remaining schedule, based on .539 opponent winning PCT.
Yao just strung together double-doubles in six consecutive games for the first time in his career . . . but T-Mac just tweaked his back for the third time this season.
Rockets dropped last week because T-Mac got hurt again. The injury is even more serious than feared, but maybe they're not out of it if the new Yao stays awhile.
If you're wondering how Rockets avoided my list of Most Disappointing Teams, it's the injuries. They have to amount to some sort of asterisk.
Did you know? Houston is actually two games over .500 -- at 29-27 -- if you throw out that 1-13 record vs. fellow Southwest Division residents.
Almost no one knows Rockets' future GM, but Daryl Morey did attend Northwestern and MIT. Which, if nothing else, leads to an obvious nickname: Rocket Scientist.
Trivia time: How many teams have a better record on the road than they do at home? Answer: This one is the only one, at 18-21 compared to 15-23 in Houston.
After seeing T-Mac and Yao go 21-10 in just 31 games together, all Houston can do is hope it just stuffed a few seasons' worth of injury problems into one season.

sac.summary: Despite going 13-2 after an 0-3 start last season, Kings really didn't want to try their luck twice. Hence their relief to pull out Sunday night's thriller in Phoenix.
I'm starting to question my pre-season wisdom of giving a nod to history and consistency to rank Kings at No. 11. Losing to NY how they did has to test the faith.

Just a hunch, but offense still might be the key for new-look Kings. They averaged only 86.0 ppg in their first five losses, and 110.3 ppg in four wins, before falling Sunday in a 106-104 heartbreaker at Seattle.

Peja has missed a few games and no King is collecting more rebounds than Bonzi's 8.5 per game, but there is some good news amid the tension: Bibby, at 25 ppg in his past six outings, is starting to warm up.
The story is unchanged in Sacto. When Kings score, they win: 110.1 ppg in seven victories. In the 10 losses? Just 89.7 ppg.

Kings recently completed their longest winless homestand (0-4) since 1992. So long ago, in other words, that we're talking some six years before anyone aorund the league started calling Arco Arena a tough place to play.
Over the past four seasons, Kings haven't won fewer than 30 games at home. Sacto can still get there this term, but it'll take a 23-4 run from here.

Here's a holiday shout-out to the Arco faithful, who keep filling every seat in the house even though Kings keep losing home games (7-8) and, of greater concern, have started losing starters (Peja and Bonzi).

It's no fun picking on a good guy like Reef, but facts are facts: Kings are 2-0 without him -- with Bibby posting back-to-back games of 30-plus points after just one game in the 30s before Sacto lost Reef, Bonzi and Peja.
The good news? Miller double-doubled in four straight after Reef got hurt. The bad news? Kings don't see Clips again until April; Sacto has won the past 11 meetings.
Kings used to be virtually automatic at home. The norm at Arco now is giving up 100 points, which, for the first time since '93, has happened in 10 straight home dates.
Good times/bad times: Routed Suns, welcomed back Peja and Reef, upped their win streak to three ... then opened a six-game trip with an OT loss at Orlando.
Even if Artest somehow gets through the rest of the season without incident, let's hold off on the playoff talk until Kings are out of last place in the Pacific.
The gamble on Artest sure didn't change Sacto's injury fortunes. Miller and Bonzi are dinged up again and even Artest is hobbling around.
The good news: With Artest, Kings are winning at home again (eight straight). The bad news: Kings play 14 of next 22 on the road between now and the end of March.
Credit where credit is due: Artest's arrival has Kings looking more likely to make a playoff push than anyone from No. 9 down in the West. So far, anyway.
Kings have won a more Kings-like nine straight at home. But Kings are 1-6 on the road since the Artest deal and play only 12 of their final 27 games at home.
They're only 11-7 since Artest arrived, but Kings seem hotter than that given the pressure they're putting on Lakers at the bottom of the West playoff ladder.
Before Friday, Kings had visited the .500 Club only once all season . . . at 7-7. Now Kings are 15-7 in the Artest Era and, as of Monday morning, suddenly up to No. 8.
I'm not prepared to pronounce Kings a threat to overtake No. 6 Memphis, but it does look safe to say that, with Artest, they're in the top eight to stay.
Kings, like Mavs, can testify that Warriors, if nothing else, haven't quit. Sacto was 11-0 at home in the Artest Era until Golden State arrived Sunday.
Hate to spoil the mood, but the West's supposed spoilers are 5-5 since a 7-1 start to March and 21-12 since the Artest trade. In other words: good, but not yet fearsome.
Tuesday's visit to Dallas was the worst performance of the Artest Era, but it's the only blip in a 6-1 run that has given Kings a shot to secure seventh in the West.
If this is his Sacto swansong, Adelman will leave Kings with eight playoff berths in eight tries. Which is why you can be sure he'll be coaching somewhere next season.

gsw.summary: As if they didn't already know it, Warriors needed only one week to reconfirm that their whole season rides on Baron's durability. They're 2-0 with him, 0-1 without him.
In their locker room after Saturday's loss in Phoenix, you'd have thought Warriors had just fallen to 1-6. But maybe that's a good sign that they're this focused already.
Baron alluded to it in our discussion in the weekend Dime: Warriors have a rough November with 17 games. The good news? Of the six left, five are at home.
Only four teams thus far have managed to avoid losing two games in a row. And Warriors are one of them, joining Pistons, Mavs and Spurs.

The level of competition, granted, hasn't been the toughest. And they do shoot way too many 3s. Warriors, though, absolutely had to start well to maintain the momentum from last season's finish. Credit them for doing so.
Warriors can rationalize a couple narrow losses to top teams (Suns and Pistons). They didn't have this many wins last season until mid-January.
As ugly as their Jersey stop was, Warriors can remember far uglier times. Like last season, for instance, when win No. 15 didn't come until Feb. 16.
After closing a five-game trip with four double-digit losses, allowing 108.8 ppg in the process, it's safe to say any momentum from the dream start is a memory.

As rough as their last road trip proved, dragging these November darlings all the way back to .500, the sight of Warriors coming from behind to win at Dallas is as impressive as anything we saw from these guys in the first month.
The prospect (threat?) of an Artest trade probably is affecting these guys and Denver more than Pacers. Indy, after all, is more accustomed to Artest-related uncertainty.
The way they're sliding now, with the team's effort perhaps waning as well, Montgomery is in trouble whether or not Warriors can complete an Artest deal.
Warriors insist their recent slump was the byproduct of a rough schedule stretch. Fine. Prove it to us with six of the next eight games at home.
Warriors are 3-9 this month and chose not to pull the trigger on an Artest deal. In the other words, Baron and Montgomery will continue to be the big story.
Everyone close to the situation says Monty's going nowhere, but the same can sadly be said about his unhappy team: Warriors are 9-19 since that 12-6 start.
Time will tell us if this was the right move. But since Warriors refused to part with Diogu in an Artest deal, the rookie bruiser is playing just 10.6 mpg in February.
As if the NBA's longest playoff drought weren't enough -- 11 seasons and counting -- Warriors also have the longest All-Star drought now: none since Spree in 1997.
They've been skidding for weeks and this won't help: No team returned from the break with a higher percentage of road games remaining than Warriors: 18 of 30.
Anyone remember that 12-6 start? Warriors are 13-27 since, which is why Monty's name is bound to start coming up for college openings.
Monty beats Heat, then loses in Orlando, adding up to zero relief on the hot seat. No wonder he just admitted: ''There are a lot of things I miss about college.''
The impact of the Weekend Dime is indisputable. Branded as the league's No. 2 disappointment, Warriors suddenly have their first two-game win streak in six weeks.
Since the Warriors have dropped out of (realistic) playoff contention, this will have to do: They can proudly say they're the only team to win twice at Dallas this season.
So how do Warriors follow up road wins over Dallas and Sacto and 10-spot rise I'd like to take back? With a four-game losing streak, three of the losses at home.
The numbers are getting gruesome by the Bay. Sixteen losses by three points or less or in overtime have dropped Warriors to 18-40 since that 12-6 start.
The league's longest playoff drought has been stretched to 12 seasons. Which tells me Warriors, in the top 10 in attendance yet again, must have the NBA's best fans.

okc.summary: Sonics Nation is undoubtedly thinking that a loss to Clips on Opening Night isn't the worst karma. Except when Supes did it last season, it wasn't at home like this time.

If they can recover to contend after this avalanche -- three consecutive losses by a combined 93 points -- it would be an even more dramatic rise to prominence than last season's. Trouble is, harmony seems a long way off here.
Well, well, well. Sonics suddenly have won four out of five and have a chance to really hush the doomsday talk with nine of the next 11 games at home.
This wasn't as bad as the week Supes lost three straight roadies by a combined 93 points. But with three more Ls and Rashard talking about free agency, it was close.
Supes gave up a lot of points in the process, as always, but back-to-back wins against visitors from the mighty Central Division (Cavs and Pacers) represent the first glimpse of last season's Sonics.
They've been better lately, but there's a reason Sonics haven't been over .500 yet: No team in the West allows more than 99 ppg ... except Seattle at 104.8.
Rolling up a 33-point lead on Nate's Blazers was fun. Hitting the 20-game mark at 9-11? Not so joyous for those who can remember last season's 17-3 start.

Conflicts with the city over the future of KeyArena and how long they'll stay are not Supes' only problems in Seattle. They've also played 15 of 25 games at home . . . but have dropped five of the past six there.
Sonics haven't been over .500 yet. Of course, it's a wonder they've gotten close with the NBA's most porous D (104.9 ppg allowed) and worst FG D (49.7 percent).
The worst news about the new coach getting called for on-court interference in Detroit? Hill's run-in with Rip was the best defensive instinct from Sonics all season.
If Sonics don't have Ray Allen in uniform -- or Jesus Shuttlesworth -- let's face it. Probably doesn't matter who the coach is in those circumstances.
Third time hasn't been so charming for Hill. After winning records as an interim coach in NY ('86) and Indy ('90), he's only 3-7 here even after Sunday's thriller in PHX.
Go ahead, suffering Sonics fans. It's OK to admit that you heard about the new assistant coach, a certain Mr. Schrempf, and wished he was coming back as a player.
Amid ownership threats that Seattle's only title-winning sports franchise might be leaving town, Sonics might register their first losing record at home since 1984-85.
Doubt he'd admit it, but I'm guessing Allen would prefer a trade this month to a team with real playoff possibilities as opposed to one All-Star Weekend in Houston.
The news just gets bleaker and bleaker in rainy Seattle: No team's winning percentage has fallen further since the end of last season than Sonics' .634 to .377.
The good news: Wilcox is off to a decent start. The better news: February is almost over, after 10 roadies this month and Sonics' 1-9 record in those games.
Says Rashard: Schultz's reluctance to spend money and the franchise's uncertain future in town have, according to Lewis, put 'that Seattle rain' over Sonics' heads.
After all those trade scenarios involving all those teams that were trying to get this guy, Watson isn't playing any more for Sonics (21 mpg) than he played in Denver.
If it's up to Ray Allen, Bob Hill stays. Hill has to like hearing that, knowing that the last guy Allen backed (Bob Weiss) also got the job.
We were still digesting the two-game eruption from Wilcox -- 46 points, 33 boards -- when this news blipped across the screen late Sunday: Sonics 106, Spurs 102.
Tough times: Wilcox averages a mere 14 and 6 in the five games after his two-game eruption ... and Hollinger brands Sonics ''worst defensive team ever.''
Schultz, like Paul Allen in Portland, gets no sympathy from the Seattle public. And I totally get it, given all the $4 coffees purchased weekly by the committee (of one).
Looks like Hill will be back on Sonics' bench, but don't ask for more info. Rashard? Wilcox? The team itself? No one's making NBA predictions in Seattle these days.

cle.summary: LeBron hasn't been the problem in Cavs' two defeats, but they do need even more from him (only 11 boards so far) with this group still getting to know each other.
Good response to a poor start. A 4-0 week, even against so-so comp, put Cavs in Team O' The Week running and merits a return to the top 10.
Cavs haven't lost a home game. They've won three in a row on the road. In other words, an LBJ squad is finally living up to the hype.
LBJ scoring 30-plus is becoming routine -- seven times already -- but the real key might be Hughes' passing. When Larry leads them in assists, Cavs are 6-0.
Ten wins in November tied a franchise record, but it'd be easier to get excited about Cavs' start if they weren't mandhandled by Spurs, Pacers and Clips, too.
Two obvious problems: Cavs aren't winning lately when LBJ scores big, and they're not playing anything close to the sort of D expected by their Pop-schooled new coach.
Eight (wins in a row) was definitely not enough. Cavs are 4-7 since and looked so jittery Saturday that they nearly let weary Miami back into a game that was over.
The new commercials are good, but real life ain't bad for LeBron. Cavs have started winning again (5-0 after a 1-5 start this month) and LBJ turns 21 by week's end.

A month that couldn't have started in much worse fashion (1-5) was capped with the ultimate flourish: LeBron's 21st birthday and a victory over Detroit. Cavs' only loss since Dec. 13 was inflicted by slightly hotter Nets.
Cavs will miss Hughes, obviously, but probably can scrape by in the short term if LBJ keeps this up: 32.5 ppg, 6.9 rpg, 6.9 apg and 51.4-percent shooting since Dec. 1.
The last time Hughes played, Cavs beat Detroit. Without him, Cavs posted an 0-4 week with a bad home loss to Knicks and three discouraging road near-misses.
Only downer about those skid-halting 51 points in Utah: LBJ played so well in those compression tights that he'll have to keep wearing them.
Told you LeBron wouldn't be able to ditch the tights. How can he? After that six-game skid, Cavs are 5-0 since he started wearing them.
Last season's Cavs got to 30-20 before a 12-20 fold dropped them all the way out of the playoffs. These Cavs are hoping Hughes' return prevents a similar fold.
Nervous time? Hughes will sit longer than expected and a home loss to shorthanded GSW looked too familiar after the two second-half swoons in the LBJ Era.
Cavs are just 13-11 without Hughes. But let's set the bar high for the All-Star Game MVP and demand no worse than a 19-11 finish from LBJ's Cavs to get to 50 wins.
We'll get to the shrewd Flip Murray pickup later. First I need to hear that reports of Cavs fans booing LeBron were indeed exaggerated. Set me straight, Cleveland.
Yes, Cleveland. Looks like I was way out of line in recent weeks to suggest that your Cavs were possibly ripe for a third successive second-half slide. I take it all back.
Cavs don't slide in this not-so-new East even when they try to. At 18-18 sans Hughes, on a mere 46-36 pace, they still have the No. 3 record in the conference.
This seems a fine time to ease up on LeBron, after a big comeback win and since he's younger than those two darlings of the college game: Morrison and Redick.
All that fuss over LeBron's game-winning J against Bobcats buried the real story: Cavs might have finally conquered their fade demons by winning five in a row.
Don't know whether surging Cavs have the gas for a 6-3 finish ... but if LeBron can get them to 50 wins, he might just force himself into the MVP reckoning.
A season-high No. 5 despite the MSG loss because (A) Knicks actually looked like an NBA team last week and (B) big Jersey win took Cavs to 8-9 against the "Super Six."
Sunday was too soon to test LeBron's ankle for my liking, but I suppose it's safe to trust the kid who still has Cavs in the running for the third-best record in the East.

min.summary: There's not much you can dissect at this juncture except to say that OT has not been kind at all to KG and Co. so far.
Wolves don't play a road game for another 10 days. Which is probably welcome news after two OT road defeats and a failure to win at depleted Denver.
It's been a decent start, but it's also pretty clear already that (A) McHale has lots to do to win back KG's support and (B) KG trade speculation is going to be a constant.
Let's see if winning in Cleveland gets Wolves going, because they were 0-4 on the road before that breakthrough and play four of the next five away.

Wolves are quietly building some confidence and swear they should be more than three games over .500. Maybe they're right, given the close nature of several losses -- back-to-back roadies in OT early and a rough loss in OKC, for instance.
They're getting no Surprise Team ink, like Clips and Suns sans Amare, but I bet KG and Co. will settle for the West's longest win streak (tied w/Dallas at five).
Nothing can halt momentum like a few narrow losses. And Wolves have more than a few, sitting at 3-7 in games decided by five points or less.
At 1-5 since a five-game win streak to open the month, Wolves might come to rue their inability to seize upon Denver's struggles and gain some divisional ground.

Remember when I wrote that Wolves need Artest to keep KG from getting discouraged? Judging by this KG quote, they'd better hurry: ''I don't make decisions around here. I guess I've just got to live with it till the summer gets here.''
Go ahead and add Wolves to the list of teams affected by Artest speculation. Minny is 3-10 since its five-game win streak and under .500 for the first time since 3-4.
Call them our anti-Bucks. Wolves have clawed back to .500, but they're a demoralizing 0-5 in games decided by three points or fewer.
A national TV audience saw firsthand why we call them the anti-Bucks. Blowing a 19-point lead to Philly dropped Minny to 0-6 in games decided by three or fewer points.
Wally was playing as well as he ever has and Wolves were two games under .500. That's why you're wrong if you say it was a trade for the sake of making a trade.
Wolves want to believe being on the road is what suddenly made them look so out of sorts. If not, their post-trade surge of momentum sure didn't last long.
I'm not expecting a very chipper KG at All-Star Weekend. Not when, even after the injection of new blood, he's been powerless to prevent a 1-6 tumble this month.
At just 4-8 with Ricky Davis, and after a 1-4 home stand, you can understand why Wolves are looking to swing one more deal before the trade buzzer.
I fear a suspension for ball-tossing KG is inevitable. What we know for sure is that KG's frustration with 12th-placed Wolves is now there for everyone to see.
I thought Wolves would be better than 7-11 with Ricky. Of course, I never thought I'd see the day that KG, at 29, misses the playoffs two seasons in a row.
The latest indignity for an apparently lottery-bound KG? Seeing Minnesota's trade partners from Boston, with Wally, make a legit playoff push now.
If you're curious about KG's short fuse lately, some background: Wolves had a lead of at least nine points in every game on their six-game trip . . . and lost all six.
On Jan. 20, Wolves were 19-18. Then they blew a 19-point lead at Philly, traded Wally for Ricky shortly thereafter and now need a 12-0 finish to wind up at .500.
The other drama for KG's Wolves? Every loss increases their odds of landing a top-10 pick. If it's lower than No. 10, it goes to Clippers (gulp) as part of the Cassell deal.
With Wolves' first-round pick going to Clips if it falls outside the top 10, and Minny holding the league's seventh-worst record, every loss helps. Sad but true.
That kind of season: Wolves sit KG and Ricky Ricky to enhance their chances of finishing in the lottery's top 10 and keeping their pick ... and win twice anyway.

nop.summary: Hornets should pay to fly me in for all of their season openers at home. They're 2-0 in the two I've covered ... with an average win margin of 25.5 points.
With Hornets coming off a season that began at 2-29, you can understand why they were so proud to be 1-0 and then 2-1. And why 2-3 is passable, too.
Tough as it is to imagine Hornets finding a way back to New Orleans, they've made it back to pesky faster than anyone expected, thanks to Paul's smooth transition.
Maybe these Hornets are even more than pesky. If ROY favorite Paul keeps getting this much help from David West, it's not impossible.
