Hornets have already matched last December's win total, at 1-1 this month compared to 1-14 in December 2004. Plus they've already been over .500 twice this season -- 1-0 and 8-7 -- which never happened last season.
Hornets are facing their first on-court crisis of the season, but, as with Warriors, it's all relative. NO-OKC didn't secure its ninth win last season until Feb. 9.

Remember when we said J.R. Smith, as a shooting guard, doesn't quite shoot it well enough for our taste? Fact is, Hornets seem almost unbeatable when Smith scores at least 16 ... but it's happened only six times (5-1).

The crowds have been big and loud, and here's another reason it'll be tough to leave their new digs in OKC: Hornets have already beaten three division leaders at home (Spurs, Clips, Wolves) as well as a virtual leader (Philly).
West's steady improvement and Paul's ongoing progress can't mask the fact that the season is getting tougher for these underdogs: 7-7 in November, 5-10 in December.
The present is suddenly painful for Hornets' much-hyped Backcourt of the Future. Paul's out for two weeks, and J.R. Smith has landed in Byron Scott's doghouse.
I don't know if it was the prudent course, but C-Paul's speedy return from torn thumb ligaments -- after sitting out just one game -- will only spawn more ROY fawning.
Folks are actually starting to ask where Hornets would stage playoff games, Which is another way of saying things are going too well to mess with Artest. Aren't they?
OK, OK. Even one week at No. 11 might have been a bit aggressive. But the question is still valid for at least another week: Will playoff games be in OKC or NO?
Byron-bashers have no choice this time but to give the man his props. Unless you think Eddie Jordan is somehow pulling the strings from Washington.
I'm officially an all-in believer in Hornets' playoff dream. They just went 2-0 without CP3 thanks to the the ever-underrated Speedy and Snyder's unexpected surge.
Logic tells you Paul's myriad injuries and rising expectations could cause young Hornets to crumble, but I'm gullible enough to believe in their Cinderella mojo.
OK, OK. Perhaps we were struck with a bit of OKC fever when we bumped Hornets all the way up to No. 7. They're still top-10ers, though.
Hornets are torn about Wednesday's emotional return to New Orleans because it takes a big away game away from their proven home-court advantage in OKC.
Each of NO/OKC's first eight opponents this month is playoff-bound. Let's just say, with an 0-5 start in those eight games, the Hornets are testing my ''all-in'' belief.
Hornets were the NBA's fairy-tale team until the All-Star break. Since then: Hornets are 2-10 overall and 0-7 in March against seven playoff-bound opponents.
What kind of March has it been for the Cinderellas of the first half? Hornets are 1-2 back home in New Orleans this month ... and 0-8 everywhere else.
Lord Byron's honesty isn't remembered fondly in Jersey, but it's working with Hornets, who are 3-0 since he said lots of them ''just quit'' in a rout at Utah.
The good news: Hornets already have as many wins this month (three) as they had in March. The bad news: Going 3-11 in March pretty much doomed them.
I know I promised playoff basketball at the so-called Arco Arena of the Midwest, but how can any Hornet fans, wherever they live, expect more than they got?

cha.summary: The first winning record in franchise history is nice. Nice, though, could (and should) be even nicer: Bobcats blew a 3-0 start with that giveaway in Chicago.
More disappointing than the losing streak is Wallace's run of injuries. Swingman's surprising start has been interrupted by a concussion and now a wrist ailment.

How unlikely was the 30-something humiliation of Indy? In just the 91st game in Bobcats history? Bear in mind that Grizz needed two home cities (two home countries, for that matter) and more than 600 games before they beat someone by 30.
Bobcats have had nine different leading scorers in 13 games, but there's no question Wallace's surprising start (18.5 ppg, .576 shooting, 2.63 spg) is the highlight so far.
No team in the league has played more road games than Charlotte's 11. And no team, sadly, has fewer road wins than Bobcats' one.
With the league's longest losing streak (seven) and 10 consecutive defeats on the road, Bobcats must be starting to long for the day when they were a plucky expansion team carrying zero expectations.
Okafor's numbers are down a bit as a sophomore, true, but the news isn't all bleak. Bobcats did just go to Jersey and win a road game, after all.
Bobcats did manage to win their first game without the injured Okafor, at Chicago, but don't get carried away. They clearly still need Mek to rush back.
It only seems as though Bobcats are playing better without Okafor. A better theory: Charlotte found a good time to see slumping Chicago twice in a short span.
As if the Okafor and Knight injuries weren't troubling enough, there's this: Wallace hasn't led Bobcats in scoring once since his Player of the Week honors in November.
When you miss eight games, then reaggravate your ankle injury in your first game back like Okafor did, you will find it hard to hush the sophomore jinx talk.
Houston ain't the only one with beaucoup injury problems. Bobcats just lost another key name when Wallace, finally looking like the November Wallace, went down again.
Bickerstaff said we could use that quote about Detroit so long as we reminded everyone that injuries are the main reason why Bobcats are 1-14 in January.
In their current state, with basically anyone you've heard of out injured, Bobcats weren't expecting to beat Lakers. The goal was simply holding Kobe under 82.
Even if Bobcats didn't just post the first three-game win streak in club history without him, Okafor resting that ankle for the rest of the season isn't the worst idea.
Don't want to make light of a car accident, but the news that Felton was injured during a weekend off is sadly no surprise in Bobcats' season of injury misery.
Give him some East Player of the Week votes: After his car accident, Felton posts two double-doubles and a 31-point game. Bobcats even went 1-2 in those games.
Bobcats have racked up so many injuries and losses lately that no one even asks any more if Okafor (ankle) plans to come back for a few games.
Would G. Wallace get more pub if he had a cooler wife? In three games before Sunday, he averaged a Kirilenko-like 19.7 ppg, 11.3 rpg, 2.7 apg, 4.7 spg, 3.0 bpg.
What do Okafor and MJ have in common? Okafor's 26 games are the fewest in Year 2 for a reigning Rookie of the Year since His Airness played 18 in 1985-86.
Villanueva's 48-point game might have sealed ROY runner-up status, but Felton has a case, too, after averaging 16.3 ppg and 6.0 apg this month.
The difference between Bobcats and the two teams below? Charlotte is still trying, as evidenced by the sudden release of Kareem Rush for not working hard enough.
It took bickering between Bickerstaff and Phil Jackson over the release of Kareem Rush, but Bobcats can finally say they've helped spark a national controversy.
Okafor wound up playing in only 26 games. Wallace has missed 26 games himself. So in the name of comment symmetry, I'm predicting two more wins for Bobcats.

chi.summary: They will not start 0-9 again, but that's all we know for sure. It's too soon to know whether to focus on the big deficit or the big comeback vs. Charlotte.

Bulls haven't won more than four games in November since MJ's last season (1997-98). It looks like this November might be different, even as the annual early-season arrival of the circus sends Chicago on the road for six.

Happy Thanksgiving, indeed. Bulls finally won one on their annual ''circus'' road trip -- to improve to 2-41 on these jaunts since 1999 -- and get a holiday break back home before finishing the six-game swing in Texas over the weekend.
Team O' The Week, for sure. Bulls not only stunned Spurs in SA; they also turned an 0-3 start into a more-than-respectable 3-3 finish on the dreaded ''circus'' trip.
It hasn't hurt them badly yet, but Bulls are shooting seven fewer free throws per game than the opposition. We bring it up, though, because chances are it'll be hard to keep winning that way.
I'd like to focus on the 6-1 record in their last seven roadies, but how can I? With another Bulls big man facing health issues, this time Chandler's breathing, I can't.
Six players average in double figures. None of them scores more than 15 ppg. Add it all up and you see that Bulls aren't just small, they're unique.

Bulls had a players-only practice, so we'll let a player comment on Chicago's inconsistency. Says Duhon: "Night in and night out, we don't know what team is going to show up - the horrible team, the mediocre team or the good team."

Bulls and Sonics were the teams we pegged for likely slippage and suddenly Chicago is slipping faster: Six straight losses, resulting in a 5-11 December, and down to No. 12 in FG defense (No. 1 last season, remember).
If smallish Bulls can recover from an eight-game skid and a 2-9 rut at home, with their declining defense, it would top last season's resurrection from an 0-9 start.
All the fuss about Gordon's role (starting or sixth man?) and future (on the block or not?) has spared Chandler from a national inquest into his anemic production.
One big reason for Bulls' struggles: Before Saturday's 15 points and 14 boards in a victory at Indy, Chandler had 10 points ... for the entire month.
A slumbering Chandler has awakened at last. Gordon is getting more consistent, too. Best of all for Bulls, you're never out of the playoff running in the East.
Bulls can only hope this Chandler stays for a while: 10-plus rebounds in six of seven games after just eight such efforts all season before this stretch.
They've addressed some longstanding road woes and Gordon recently scored 30-plus in three straight, but Bulls ain't going to the playoffs if they stay sub-.500 at home.
If the target is making a push for the No. 8 slot, Chicago's nightly target has to be triple digits. The last 20 times they were held under 100 points, Bulls are 2-18.
Buying out T. Thomas to let him sign with Nets is one thing. You can understand why Bulls don't want to buy him out so Thomas can help keep Philly in the top eight.
A playoff berth remains a maybe at best, even with Hinrich and Gordon scoring freely these days, but Bulls can bank on a thank-you note from Phoenix for T. Thomas.
Bulls aren't even the biggest threat to No. 8 Bucks these days -- it's Boston -- but it's not Deng's fault. He's averaging 17.4 ppg and 11.3 rpg in his last seven.
Going to Milwaukee and losing a huge game by 16 only adds to the perception that Bulls don't have a run in them. But Philly's slide gives them a new team to chase.
Bulls were 5-7 in February. They were 4-8 in March until winning two in a row. Yet they are just a game and a half out of eighth place in this less-than-beastly East.
Bulls began their latest playoff ''push'' with a home loss last Tuesday to Orlando, but they sure picked the right race to be in because Philly keeps giving Chicago life.
Failed to kill off Philly, but Bulls are still sitting prettiest when compared to Bucks, Pacers and Sixers. 'Cause they get Knicks' No. 1 pick no matter what happens.
I was as frustrated as Skiles by losing records in Feb. and March, but we all must concede that Bulls are deservedly playoff-bound. A 10-2 run is hardly backing in.

phi.summary: Sixers can only hope Dalembert is an All-World defender. Because they're giving up 111 ppg without him, even after winning in Indy.
Nowitzki's injury departure Wednesday was good fortune, but credit Sixers for building on that break with a couple of quality follow-up triumphs over Lakers and Clips.
With Iverson in MVP form and Webber looking worlds more comfortable beside him -- and a second AI playing sticky D -- that 0-3 start seems like forever ago.

Eighty-five Iverson points in Sixers' last two games netted zero victories. It's no mystery why, either: Philly's porous D, which doesn't seem to be getting any better, surrendered 213 points in the two defeats.
Only once in this 2-7 skid has Iverson been held under 30 points. Strangely, though, it happened in one of the two games Philly won.
One of the toughest teams to read so far. Yet this much is certain: One tutorial from Moses Malone isn't nearly enough to drastically improve Philly's rebounding.
Yes, you read right. In the surprise development no one's talking about, board-hungry Sixers got 12 and 10 in consecutive games from one Shavlik Randolph.
After a 6-1 uptick, Team Up And Down has to be a bit worried. Sixers don't come home until Jan. 9 and lost the first of seven straight roadies at ATL despite AI's 53.
If current form holds, Sixers probably won't mind an upcoming schedule that doesn't have them facing an East foe until Jan. 13. They're 8-4 against the West.
Devastating as his scoring can be, Iverson is still best when he's also a passer. Sixers are 14-8 when AI has at least six assists, 2-9 when he dishes five or fewer.
One more shot from Iverson on Dec. 18 and he'd have broken Rick Barry's record for most consecutive games to start a season with at least 20 shots: 35 in 1974-75.
Team of the Week? Try Roller Coaster of the Week, with Webber and Iverson blowups, then the OT win over Memphis and the comeback in Minny.
Could all the problems and tension be eased by some consistent rebounding? Sixers are 17-2 when they outboard the opposition, but it happens less than half the time.
Relax, panicky Philly fans. It has been a rocky season up to now, true, but recent history offers this for optimism: Webber hasn't missed the playoffs since 1998.
Perhaps we were premature with the ''relax'' advice. Too many losses and too much unhappiness lately have plunged Sixers into another worrying slide.
It's looking like a no-win stretch run. From where they are now, Sixers have to worry about missing the playoffs and the prospect of getting swept by Detroit in Round 1.
Philly's consolation from the All-Star Saturday robbery: A ticked-off Iguodala has had two 20-point games since Houston, after going 21 games without one.
Like a lot of you, I'm saddened that Team USA didn't bring back its greatest patriot. But the snub is helping Sixers, with Iverson pouring it on in this 5-2 uptick.
A long-term Iverson injury means Philly's season is toast . . . or that Sixers will make the playoffs without him to set up the loudest summer yet of Trade AI chatter.
A 1-0 start without Iverson is suddenly a 1-4 slide without Iverson. Add that to Nets' (latest) rebound and there goes any shot at the division title.
Sixers are lucky Bulls dropped four in a row in the midst of Philly's 2-9 swoon. And there's more good fortune amid the gloom: Sixers will see Knicks twice this week.
Since that March 5 home collapse vs. Indy, Sixers are 4-9. What's left of Philly's lead goes if it can't win at least one of this week's two Sixers-Bulls ''showdowns.''
Winning at Chicago, without Webber, kept the dream alive (if you can call it that). But here's the reality: Sixers have only two home games left and four away.
The E isn't for Easter, it's for Elimination. Iverson and Webber both played more than 70 games and, amazingly, that might not even be good enough for the No. 9 spot.

bos.summary: They've been to OT twice already and lost another game at the buzzer. So they're young and exciting, at least for starters.
So they can't beat Duncan's Spurs. So what? Celts can live with a 16th loss in a row to S.A. when it's sandwiched between wins over Memphis and Houston.
If Celts can regularly reproduce the ball they've played against Detroit, maybe these guys (and kids) will be able to hang around for a while in the Titanic, er, Atlantic.

The math is a bit gruesome, as our man Peter May wrote Sunday. Celts' five wins have come against teams with a combined record of 22-46. They're also 0-4 on the road and 0-6 in both ends of their three back-to-backs sets.

Celts have tortured my man Simmons with that 6-8 showing in November, especially with 10 of those 14 games at home.  But here's, well, something: Boston is 4-0 against fellow Titanic Division opposition.
Thanks to Rockets' win at Sacto on Thursday night, only one team in the league has failed to win two in a row at least once. That would be Celts.
Five roadies follow these next two at home. In other words, the only team out there that hasn't won two in a row yet might have to wait until 2006 to break through.

We've been on Celts plenty for taking so long to win two in a row, but here's the flip side: Boston is one of only five teams this season not to lose three in a row . . . and the other four are all top-tenners: Pistons, Mavs, Spurs and Indy.

This will probably only serve to make teams more interested in trying to trade for him -- especially when Artest relinquishes top spot in the speculation game -- but Pierce has never looked better. Has he?
Celts' defense is getting leakier, and they don't win the close ones: 10 of their 20 losses are by five or fewer points. As a result, fan discontent with Doc is rising.
If you like speculation above all else, this is your team. Because now, on top of the never-ending Pierce chatter, calls for a coaching change are a constant, too.
Not what my man Simmons or any other Boston Sports Fan wants to hear right now, especially so soon after Patriots' demise ... but Ainge says Doc is going nowhere.
I realize Ricky was popular, and that Wally's no stopper, but I'd say a highly efficient scorer with a killer outside touch fits better next to Pierce than Davis did.
At least Wolves had a little momentum immediately after the Ricky-for-Wally trade. Celts just played five games in the space of seven days and lost them all.
It's been that kind of season: Perkins posts four straight double-digit rebound games after only six all season . . . then suffers a dislocated shoulder in practice.
Danny Ainge has said Celts are just a move or two away from East contention. I'm pretty sure he said so knowing that cloning Larry Bird is not an option.
Pierce is the league's top scorer in February at 33.5 ppg. Now for the real news: Celts just went 3-1 on a four-game trip after leaving home with a 4-20 road record.
Something else that's not Pierce's fault? Celts are still the only team in the league without a single three-game win streak this season.
Props to Pierce not only for doing something Bird never did -- 30 points or more in seven straight games -- but for elevating his game at the most important time.
After all those 30-point games -- with a bad elbow, no less -- not even Pierce could spare Celts from that big blown lead in Miami, then a loss at lowly Orlando.
Bye-bye, playoffs: Pierce has managed to score 30 only three times in the past 10 games, and Celts still haven't won three in a row this season.
It's not an easy East for everybody: Since Pierce told his teammates they'd need a 15-6 finish to reach the playoffs, Celts are 4-8.
Playoffs? Playoffs? The real question with Celts still looking for their first three-game win streak: Where's Jim Mora when you need him?
Celts indeed made it all the way through the season without a single three-game win streak. More troubling, though: Big Al Jefferson didn't take that big step forward.

por.summary: The good news: Blazers' next road game isn't until Nov. 20. The bad news: Blazers are scoring just a basket more per game than Orlando.
If you wish to claim that you expected Nate's new team to start faster than his old team, go ahead. But we don't believe you.
Microfracture patient Randolph has posted six double-doubles in Portland's first eight games. Which might mean as much to Phoenix (and Amare) as it does to Blazers.
The whole Patterson flap dredges up tiresome images of chaos, but sitting at 2-3 on a seven-game trip ain't bad for a team still waiting for its first 100-point night.
Dare we say it's time for NBA TV to stop running that commercial in which Patterson and Nate are joking around in practice. That has to be training camp footage.
Before 2005-06, Portland had never lost two games in one season by 39-plus points. And with one of their few vets (Miles) hurt now, Blazers have to brace for more lows.
The first of many questions McMillan has to be asking himself by now: Will we ever score 100 points? Six times so far, Blazers haven't even reached 80.
Blazers almost scored 100 twice, then they almost won at Detroit. So maybe Portland was due for a breakthrough, even without the injured D-Miles, when it won at Minny.

Is it really this simple? As young and shorthanded as they are without D-Miles, Blazers are 8-4 when Randolph scores at least 20 points. Then again ... shouldn't Zach be scoring in the 20s more regularly?
Blake? Telfair? Just start the guy who best puts Randolph in position to score 20 because Blazers win when it happens (8-4) ... but it doesn't happen enough.
Don't like to nitpick after three straight wins, but Portland is still just 8-4 when Zach scores 20. Which means Zach hasn't had a 20-point game since 2005. Why?
Giving my Zach rants a rest this week has enabled me to notice that, hey, Nate's Blazers have pretty much caught his old team in the standings, too.
Going 5-3 on an eight-game homestand, as young as Blazers are, ain't bad. The bad news? Eight of Portland's next 10 games are roadies.
The week wasn't a total loss for Paul Allen teams. Blazers' 2-2 showing finally gave them more wins this season than Seahawks, who topped out at 15-4.
After a 7-4 stretch in which three of the losses were close ones to good teams -- Mavs, Nuggets, Spurs -- Blazers are suddenly getting blown out everywhere they go.
I'll go out on a limb and guess that, given all the image problems in Portland in recent years, Rodman's claim that Blazers offered a tryout is probably a fabrication.
I'll go out on another limb and bet that billionaire Paul Allen struggles for sympathy from the locals in search of government assistance with Blazer debts.
With his last 11 losses coming by an average of 19.5 points, only solace for McMillan is that Blazers are only 3 1/2 games shy of Pacific Northwest bragging rights.
To be even more honest, I'd have expected to see public sympathy for the owner's financial ''woes'' before seeing offensively challenged Blazers outrun Suns.
Ongoing fall from prominence might drop Blazers all the way to No. 30 if this keeps up: 131 points total in back-to-back losses last week to Bulls and Nets.
Blazers trail McMillan's old team by 8 1/2 games with 12 to play. It's thus pretty safe to say that Pacific Northwest bragging rights will belong to Seattle.
Blazers have four wins since Feb. 1 ... in 30 tries. Which means I can't even put them ahead of a Knicks team that had four wins in March.
Reality keeps biting the new coach: Blazers clinched the West's worst record on April 2 ... with a 39-point loss to Nate's old (lottery-bound) team in Seattle.
With Miles in sabotage mode until Blazers trade him, it's painful to admit I used to be a huge fan. Doubly painful: The NBA's iffy future in the once-proud Pacific Northwest.

nyk.summary: With an 0-3 start and the next six games on the road out West, is it too early to say Larry misses Pistons more than they miss him?
The last 0-5 start Larry endured before this one wound up 43-39 (Philly in 2001-02). Even after the Sacto breakthrough, 43 wins still seems rather optimistic.
Larry and Steph need to hush. They've both done way too much complaining for guys who knew exactly what they were getting into. And 3-7, frankly, looks OK after 0-5..

We interrupt our regularly scheduled Larry vs. Steph update to point out a slightly more upbeat development: In spite of Larry's legendary reluctance to play rookies, Frye has scored at least 20 points in four of his past five games.
Larry probably deserves a grace period that lasts longer than a month. By week's end, Knicks will have played just six of 20 games at home.
The bright side of starting the season with a flurry of games in the West: Knicks don't have to travel farther away than Texas for the next four months.
No team in the United States is worse at home these days. So playing the next three at MSG might not be such great news for our pal Larry.
That seven-game skid wasn't the longest run of misery in Larry's coaching career -- he lost 13 in a row once -- but it leaves us little choice: Knicks hit bottom.

Can't say it any more bluntly than Professor Hollinger did the other day: ''Has there ever been a team in any sport that spent more to accomplish less?'' Knicks' payroll, remember, approaches $120 million . . . not including the coach.
So what can so suddenly make Larry and Steph look (somewhat) harmonious and spark a 3-0 week? Two straight humbling weeks at No. 30, that's what.
After a rough 2005, the new year is going so well that even the famously pessimistic Larry Brown has to smile. Wins over Suns, Cavs and Mavs will do that.
He might not be the best point guard in the league, as Steph famously claimed last season, but Knicks are clearly worse without him. A lot worse.
Last week was simply not a good week to be an Isaiah . . . or an Isiah. It's ugly for Knicks on the court again and even more uncomfortable off it.
Larry's first Philly team went 31-51. With all the turmoil swirling these days, it's hard to see these Knicks getting to 30 wins no matter how many trades they make.
Larry's first Spurs team went 21-61. But that team knew it was getting David Robinson in Year 2. Knicks might not win seven more, and no Admiral is on deck.
Probably no one remembers this now, with Knicks at 2-16 since Larry's 1,000th victory, but they were 6-0 in their first six games of 2006. Somehow.
The focus is bound to shift now from trades to Isiah's future, but I'm not so sure it's a slam-dunk that Zeke goes before the coach. It is Larry Brown, after all.
They have a 3-22 record since Larry's 1,000th victory, but don't fret. Dolan said -- 30-something times in one sitting -- that Knicks also do have a ''strategy.''
If this guy is so untouchable in trade talks, Isiah, shouldn't he be more playable than Larry makes it seem? Frye is averaging just 4.2 ppg in 15.8 mpg this month.
Tough to say anything good can come from Larry vs. Steph public sparring, but I do agree that the weeklong mess lit a much-needed fire under the downcast coach.
Losing Frye was pure bad luck. Trading for Steve Francis, going back to Orlando and playing him zero minutes after the first quarter defies explanation.
No matter how bad it gets, ESPN research ace Michael Jackson always wants to talk Knicks. Which always makes me wonder: Do Knicks care as much as he does?
Even after Crawford's heroics, Knicks still need two more wins, on top of this three-game win streak, to avoid tying the worst record in club history.
Mr. Billups hears the jokes about his old coach not being able to stomach Knicks' plight and had this to say about their first 60-loss season ever: 'It's not funny.'

orl.summary: Winning without Grant Hill is obviously a problem, but the first step is learning how to score without Grant Hill. Magic are at a measly 80.7 ppg so far.
The consolation for the league's lowest-scoring team? Magic, at 84.3 ppg, are staying in games with a much-improved defense (89.3 ppg allowed, down from 101.8).

It won't make a 1-4 home record any more comforting, but Magic have to be encouraged by Howard's progress (15.7 ppg, 12.7 rpg). Especially with the other stars from his draft class (Okafor and Gordon) finding Year 2 tougher.
Brian Hill's Princeton offense hasn't quite been embraced, but the consolation for the new coach is three straight Ws and the NBA's stingiest defense (88.5 ppg allowed).
Not exactly a news flash: Take Francis away from a team already without Grant Hill and Magic probably won't win much no matter what their manchild D-Howard does.
The recent 0-5 slide was a blow, but Magic can't be too down given Howard's progress and Grant Hill's expected return this week.
Even with a half-speed Grant Hill, Orlando looks like more of a team than forecasted. There's certainly nothing wrong, durability aside, with a Hill-and-Howard front line.
Rumbles and grumbles that the venerable Mr. Hill is shooting too much? A pass-first, team-first guy like Grant? I don't believe what I'm hearing.
Three straight wins. Three straight games of 100-plus points for a team that doesn't average 90. Maybe the grumblers realized Grant's return is a good thing.
Retirement is suddenly on Hill's mind, but no one's rooting harder for his swift return than Howard, who desperately needs Hill's playmaking to get to the playoffs.
As more than one Magic fan has reminded me in the wake of the Francis suspension, the locals don't refer to this franchise as the Orlando Tragic without good cause.
Slick trick from Magic management, which unsuspended Francis and assured him he won't be traded. Not a tough promise to make when interest is so low.
Poof. Just like that, Magic's unexpected five-game win streak has been followed up by losses to chaos-infested Knicks and Iverson-less Sixers.
No one needed a win over Boston more than Howard, who had to halt that four-game skid if he hoped to beat out guys like Pierce for an All-Star spot.
And then there was one: Magic's 1-7 slide makes you think that Chicago is the only team outside the East's top eight capable of making a playoff push.
Magic can only hope they do manufacture a Francis trade this week because he won't become any less of a handful if he's stuck in Orlando past Thursday's deadline.
Coach Hill insists he didn't relish the opportunity to waive Penny. But with Magic mired in a 2-13 slide, it's pretty much the only feeling of triumph he's had lately.
Bleak as day-to-day life must be for a team that has dropped 17 of 19, Magic can honestly say that Dwight and Darko look better than OK together.
Encouraging as it is to finally see some life from Darko, it's still sad when you see nights like Friday: Grant Hill trying to play and lasting just seven-plus minutes.
Stevie Franchise returns Wednesday to the O-rena. Just a hunch, but I'm guessing Magic, though just 5-9 since the trade, are happier with results so far.
The bigger surprise? You decide: Dwight Howard dropped from the starting lineup for disciplinary reasons ... or young, rebuilding Magic going 6-0 at home this month?
Brian Hill insists that his Magic are still in the playoff hunt. As limp as Sixers and Bulls look, it might not even be an exaggeration.
Chicago and Philly have been so meek in their so-called race for No. 8 that Magic -- now on a 12-4 run after winning at Miami -- deserve it no matter where they finish.
Climbing from the depths of 20-40? The possibility of a 9-0 April? Playoffs or not, Grant Hill is so geeked to play with these kids that he's talking comeback again.

atl.summary: Three roadies out West -- two routs and a one-point defeat -- add up to a tough first assignment for young, mourning Hawks.
Can't see Spree really wanting to play here even if there are no other offers. Not with so many small forwards in Atlanta and not a lot of short-term hope.
Joe Johnson goes back to the desert Dec. 4. If Hawks don't win one between now and then -- including a Dec. 2 home date with Raps -- they'll take an 0-15 record to PHX.
Can't explain how the last winless team suddenly wins two in a row. Also can't explain why the Boston win, Hawks' 10th game, was their first game against an East foe.

If there's any short-term silver lining for Joe Johnson, it's this: At least he got the Phoenix game out of the way early. Imagine how uncomfortable it would have been going back in January or February with a much uglier record than 2-13.

You probably won't see a more surprising scoreline all season than the one coming Saturday night out of Philips Arena. You also get the feeling that, without stunning Spurs, Woodson wouldn't have lasted until the next Power Rankings.
If they'd have known widespread talk of Woodson's demise would lead to a win over SA and a 4-1 run, Hawks probably would have spread the rumors themselves.
Big rematch with Raps, after losing Round 1, comes Wednesday in Toronto. And if Hawks can win two out of three this week, they secure a winning December.
Before a couple of narrow Ls last week, Hawks were actually 5-1 when leading with five minutes to go. The problem, of course, is getting those late leads more often.
On second thought, perhaps Hawks shouldn't be slammed for losing three in a row -- and two in one week -- to a Toronto team that's 10-8 since a 1-15 start.
Only one team has fewer than 10 victories and this is it. But here's a surprise: Hawks were somehow leading the league in 3-point percentage until this week.
There was never any great fear someone would challenge the all-time futility record of 9-73. Hawks are relieved just the same to make it official.
Since we always like to keep it positive, as everyone knows, we have elected to focus on Joe Johnson becoming the 12th player this month to post a 40-point game.
Can't help it. Even when Hawks are winning three in a row for the first time in almost two years, all I can do is imagine how good CP3 would look next to Joe Johnson.
OK, OK. Even I can give it a (week's) rest on the Passing Over Paul stuff when Hawks are the only team besides Mavs and Wiz to have wins over Spurs and Pistons.
He didn't get a Houston invite, but you'd have to agree that Joe Johnson -- with two game-winning shots and a triple-double -- is having an All-Star Feb. Wouldn't you?
At least one of these kids is getting it: Joe Johnson adds a 40-point game to his fabulous February and pushes his assist average for the month to 9.1.
Blowing that lead in Miami was a downer, but Hawks can comfort themselves with thoughts of a 6-6 February . . . and wins over Pistons, Nets, Lakers and Pacers.
We always use this line with Toronto, so why not with Atlanta for once: Throw out Hawks' unsightly 0-9 start and they're a rather respectable 20-31.
As the season deepens, Johnson looks more and more like a $70 million man. In March, he's averaging 27.4 ppg and 8.4 apg.
Losing Salim Stoudamire for the rest of the season (elbow) leads to (one more) painful admission: Hawks just lost their most productive rookie.
Hawks, I'm told, already have called the league office to make the request: More than four games against Indiana next season, please!
Getting snubbed for the Rookies vs. Sophs game at All-Star Weekend has turned my new favorite lefty, Josh Smith, into a new man. Now it's Marvin Williams' turn.
Hawks have only 12 more wins with Joe Johnson than they had without him. But I see the seedlings of something here nonetheless, starting with J.J. and Josh Smith.

tor.summary: Interesting. Now that the games have started, I haven't been getting as many ''You're crazy to put Toronto that low'' e-mails.

One hurting Raps fan wrote in to suggest that he'd take a point for Sunday's Seattle loss like Leafs get for OT defeats. You can understand the cynicism/desperation, given that five of Toronto's first six games were at home.
Raps owed the committee something special after sending our beloved Pape to the NBDL. All credit to them, though, because beating Miami qualifies.

I'm guessing none of my Canadian friends will be terribly surprised to read here about Pape Sow's 40 -- yes, FORTY -- points in an NBDL game Sunday. I'm guessing some Raps fans out there won't even mind.
Had they held a late lead vs. Dallas, Raps might have been Team O' The Week. But Raps did go from a five-win pace to a 14-win pace by winning at Hawks and Nets.
Why would Bosh want to leave for L.A., Phil? Raps have won three of five ... and one of the losses (Washington) came in OT.
Maybe Raps should have stayed on the road. Seriously. Last four roadies: Toronto went 3-1, only losing an OT game. This month's four home games: Toronto is 0-4, losing by an average of nearly 15.
You can't forget the 1-15 start or ignore the 1-11 record against the West. But it's time to recognize that Raps, like Hawks, are a rather respectable 5-6 this month.
The 7-7 record since a 1-15 start? Pleasantly surprising. Six wins on the road and just two at home? Perplexing is a good word.
Way up here? It's a must when my Raps average 110 ppg in stretching their win streak to five and wipe out two second-half deficits of 10-plus points.
Didn't really expect Raps to make it two straight weeks in the teens. But they have -- helped by this week's upbeat words from Bosh about sticking around.
You're not alone. We, too, wondered whether the Pape Sow recall from the D-League was made solely to persuade the committee (of one) to keep Raps in the teens.
Could be another of my crazy theories, but maybe Raps fired Babcock one day after Pape made his first start because they figured we'd be too Sow-centric to notice.
Babcock is ousted and Jalen is traded shortly thereafter, which naturally makes you wonder: Is Rafael Araujo, long protected by Babcock, at risk for a D-League stint?
Maybe Kobe did get some help from that Raps defense on the way to Eighty-One. Toronto just gave up 125 points to Spurs . . . who were playing without Duncan.
Raps haven't exactly been Mav-like since surrendering Kobe's 81, but they're a decent 5-3 this month, with two OT defeats and last week's two-point loss in NYC.
They'd look even smarter if they could've held Saturday's 24-point lead, but spending three off nights in Bosh's hometown of Dallas proves Raps ain't dummies.
After six straight excruciating defeats -- three in OT -- Raps cap a big week in franchise history by adding a W over Boston to success in the Colangelo tug-of-war.
Landing Bryan Colangelo was an undeniable credibility coup, but Raps' 2-8 record since the All-Star break is just a small example of how big his new job is.
Raptors' goal with 16 games to go? I'm guessing a 10-6 finish. Why? Because that'll put them at .500 for the season -- 33-33 -- if you throw out the 1-15 start.
How much can UConn endure? In the space of a few hours Sunday, Huskies lose to George Mason ... and Charlie Villanueva's 48 points go for naught in Milwaukee.
Thank you, Toronto. The committee (of one) is touched to report that we haven't received one e-mail attacking our man Pape for the Bosh injury.
James has scored 30-plus points in six of 11 games, but Bosh-less Raps are 1-10 in that span. So James' scoring spree might not be helping his free-agent prospects.
Raps started 1-15 and they're finishing on a 2-11 slide. But at least they had the good fortune to land a proven GM (Colangelo) in between.
